title: A prayer to pull down Celsus’s conceit
english: It is not in pursuit of the much speaking that is forbidden, the speaking from which there is no escaping “sin” (Proverbs 10:19), that we now begin a fifth book against Celsus’s treatise, holy Ambrose. It is because, as far as our strength allows, we are trying to let nothing he has said pass untested, and above all those points where some might think he has brought a shrewd charge against us or against the Jews.

If it were possible for us to enter, with our argument, into the conscience of every single person who reads his treatise, to draw out each arrow that wounds anyone not fully fenced with the whole armour of God (Ephesians 6:11), and to apply a medicine of reason to heal the wound Celsus deals, the wound that keeps those who attend to his words from being sound “in the faith” (Titus 1:13), we would have done so.

But this is God’s work: to come and dwell invisibly, by his own Spirit together with the Spirit of Christ, in those in whom he judges he ought to dwell. Our part, since we try through words and writings to bring people to faith, is to do everything so that we may be called workmen who have no cause for shame, rightly handling “the word of truth” (2 Timothy 2:15). And one part of that “everything,” it seems to us, is to refute Celsus’s plausible arguments as far as we can, faithfully carrying out the task you have set us. So come: let us set out what follows the words of Celsus to which we have already replied (whether we also overturned them, the reader will judge), and let us add our answer to it.

May God grant that our mind and our speech come to the task not bare and stripped of divinity, “so that the faith” of those we pray may be helped “may not rest in the wisdom of men” (1 Corinthians 2:5). Having received “the mind of Christ” (1 Corinthians 2:16) from his Father, who alone gives it, and being helped to share in the Word of God, may we cast down “every height that is lifted up against the knowledge of God” (2 Corinthians 10:5), and with it the conceit of Celsus, who lifts himself up against us and against our Jesus, and against Moses and the prophets as well; so that, as he who gives “a word to those who preach the good news with great power” (Psalm 68:11) supplies this to us also and grants the great power, faith may come about in those who will read this, in the word and power of God (1 Corinthians 2:4–5).
translator_notes: ‘The much speaking that is forbidden … no escaping sin’ quotes Proverbs 10:19 LXX (ἐκ πολυλογίας οὐκ ἐκφεύξῃ ἁμαρτίαν); ‘that is forbidden’ renders the participle ἀπηγορευμένην, whose source is that verse (the Greek does not name Scripture as the subject, so none is added). ‘Sound in the faith’ = Titus 1:13 (also Titus 2:2). Ephesians 6:11 (also 6:13) for πανοπλία τοῦ θεοῦ. 2 Timothy 2:15 is paraphrased into Origen’s syntax (ἐργάτας ἀνεπαισχύντους, ὀρθοτομοῦντας τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας). LXX Psalm 67:12 (κύριος δώσει ῥῆμα τοῖς εὐαγγελιζομένοις δυνάμει πολλῇ) = English Psalm 68:11; the Hebrew-based English verse reads differently. The closing ‘faith … in the word and power of God’ completes the 1 Corinthians 2:5 citation (ἀλλ᾿ ἐν δυνάμει θεοῦ) and echoes 2:4; 1 Thessalonians 1:5 is a possible secondary echo, not cited. ‘(πρὸς) τὸ προκείμενον’: πρὸς is Koetschau’s supplement, followed. The stray full stop after ὠφεληθῆναι in the staged text is a punctuation artefact and is ignored. ἐπαιρομένου agrees with Κέλσου, so it is Celsus (not his conceit) who ‘lifts himself up’. ἐπιδημεῖν rendered ‘come and dwell’.

title: Celsus says no God comes down
english: Our task now, then, is to overturn his statement, which runs as follows: “No god, O Jews and Christians, and no son of God has come down, or would come down. But if you speak of certain angels, what do you call them: gods, or some other kind of being? Some other kind, presumably: the demons.”

Celsus is repeating himself here (for he has said these things many times already above), so there is no need to discuss them at greater length; what we have said on the point will suffice. Out of many things we shall set out a few, which we think agree with what was said before, yet do not carry entirely the same sense. In them we shall show that, by declaring universally that no god or son of God has come down to men, he does away both with what the multitude believe about the appearing of a god and with what he himself said earlier.

For if the statement Celsus has made universally, “No god and no son of God has come down, or would come down,” is true, then plainly it is ruled out that there are gods on earth, come down from heaven either to give oracles to men or to heal them through oracles. Then neither the Pythian god nor Asclepius nor any other of those believed to do such things could be a god who came down from heaven. Or else he would be a god, but one who had always had the earth as his allotted dwelling, like an exile from the place of the gods; or he would be one of those who have no right to share in the company of the divine beings there. Or else Apollo and Asclepius, and all who are believed to do anything on earth, would not be gods but some kind of demons, far worse than those wise men among mankind who, by their virtue, ascend even to the vault of heaven.
translator_notes: Celsus’s words (θεὸς μὲν … τοὺς δαίμονας) are quoted again and answered in 5.4–5. ‘No son of God’ renders θεοῦ παῖς οὐδείς; lowercase ‘son’ because this is Celsus’s generic denial, while θεοῦ is kept as ‘God’ since he is denying the Christian claim. δαίμονες rendered ‘demons’ for consistency with the rest of this translation; in Celsus’s mouth the word is neutral, and Origen contests that in 5.5. ‘The Pythian god’ = Apollo of Delphi (ὁ Πύθιος; ‘god’ supplied from the article’s sense). ‘The vault of heaven’ (ἡ ἁψὶς τοῦ οὐρανοῦ) echoes Plato, Phaedrus 247b (ἡ ὑπουράνιος ἁψίς); an echo, not a quotation, so not cited inline. ‘Appearing of a god’ renders θεοῦ ἐπιφάνεια (pagan epiphany). No Scripture in this chapter.

title: Celsus caught deserting to Epicurus
english: Notice, then, that in his wish to do away with our teaching, this man, who never admitted anywhere in his treatise that he was an Epicurean, is caught deserting to Epicurus. Now is the time for you who read Celsus’s words and agree with what he sets before you: either deny that God comes to dwell among men, caring for human beings one by one, or, if you hold that he does, show Celsus’s argument to be false.

If you do away with providence altogether, you will make false those words of his in which he affirms gods and providence, just so that you can say that this statement is true. But if you hold to providence none the less, as one who does not agree with Celsus when he says that neither a god nor a son of God has come down or comes down to men, why will you not examine carefully, from what we have said about Jesus and from what was prophesied about him, whom one ought rather to believe to be God and Son of God come down to men? Is it Jesus, who arranged and accomplished so much? Or is it those who, under the pretext of oracles and divinations, do not set right the character of those they heal, who have besides fallen away from the pure and unmixed reverence owed to the Maker of the universe, and who, under the pretext of honouring many gods, split the souls of those who attend to them away from the one and only manifest and true God?
translator_notes: The second ‘you’ clause (ἢ τιθέντι … ψευδοποιεῖν) is a dative participle agreeing with σοι; rendered as an imperative pair for clarity, the either/or kept. ‘This statement’ (ταῦτα … ἀληθῆ) = Celsus’s claim that no god comes down. τῶν θεραπευομένων read as passive, ‘those they heal’, picking up διὰ χρησμῶν θεραπεύσωσι in 5.2; a middle sense ‘those who serve them’ is possible but less likely. ‘God and Son of God’ capitalised because Origen’s question points to Jesus, though grammatically the phrase is the term in dispute. ‘Arranged’ renders οἰκονομήσαντα (arranged, carried out a dispensation). No Scripture in this chapter.

title: Angels serve, but prayer goes to God
english: After this, as though Jews or Christians would answer that those who come down to men are angels, he says, “But if you speak of certain angels,” and goes on to ask, “what do you call them: gods, or some other kind of being?” Then again he brings them in as if they had answered, “Some other kind, presumably: the demons.” Come, let us consider this too.

For we too do indeed acknowledge that there are angels, who are “ministering spirits, sent out for service for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation” (Hebrews 1:14). They ascend, bringing men’s petitions up to the purest regions of the world, the heavenly ones, or even to the regions above the heavens, which are purer still; and they come down again from there, bringing to each, as he deserves, something of what God commands them to minister to those who receive the benefit. Since we have learned to call them angels from the work they do, we find that, because they are divine, they are sometimes even named “gods” in the sacred Scriptures. Yet this is not so that we should be commanded to revere and worship, in place of God, those who minister to us and bring us the things of God.

For every supplication and prayer and intercession and thanksgiving (1 Timothy 2:1) must be sent up to the God who is over all, through the High Priest who is above all the angels, the living Word and God. And we shall make supplication to the Word himself also, and intercede with him, and give thanks to him, and pray to him too, if we can understand how the word “prayer” is used in its strict sense and in its looser sense.
translator_notes: Celsus’s three phrases from 5.2 are quoted again and kept in double quotation marks. Hebrews 1:14 is quoted in pieces (λειτουργικὰ … πνεύματα, εἰς διακονίας ἀποστελλόμενα διὰ τοὺς μέλλοντας κληρονομεῖν σωτηρίαν); LXX/NT wording matches. The four terms δέησις, προσευχή, ἔντευξις, εὐχαριστία follow 1 Timothy 2:1 in order, so cited as a clear allusion. ‘Named gods in the sacred Scriptures’: Origen gives no text; likely candidates are Psalms where the LXX reads ‘angels’ for Hebrew ’elohim or where the gods are called to worship (e.g. LXX Psalm 96:7 = English 97:7; LXX 137:1 = English 138:1; Psalm 82:1 = LXX 81:1), but none is certain, so none is cited inline. ‘The High Priest who is above all the angels’ echoes Hebrews (2:17; 4:14; with 1:4 for superiority to angels); a general echo, not cited inline. ἐμψύχου λόγου rendered ‘living Word’ (literally ‘ensouled’, i.e. a living, personal Word, not a spoken word). The angels-as-messengers wordplay (ἄγγελοι from their ἔργον) is noted here rather than added to the text. ἐν τοῖς καθαρωτάτοις … χωρίοις read with late Greek ἐν for εἰς after a verb of motion. On ‘strict and looser use’ of ‘prayer’, compare Origen, On Prayer 15 (prayer in the strict sense to the Father alone).

title: Why angels are not called demons
english: For it is not reasonable to call upon angels without first acquiring a knowledge of them that is beyond human reach. And even supposing that this knowledge of them, wonderful and secret as it is, were attained, that very knowledge, by showing what their nature is and what task each of them is appointed to, will not allow anyone to venture to pray to any other than the God over all, who suffices for all things, through our Saviour, the Son of God. He is the “Word” (John 1:1), and Wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:24), and Truth (John 14:6), and all else that the writings of God’s prophets and of Jesus’ apostles say of him.

For the holy angels of God to be gracious to us and to do everything on our behalf, it is enough that our disposition toward God should imitate, as far as human nature can, their purpose, as they imitate God; and that our understanding of his Son, the Word, so far as we can attain it, should not be at odds with the holy angels’ clearer understanding of him, but should press on toward it every day in clearness and precision.

Celsus, as one who has not read our sacred Scriptures, answers himself as if speaking for us, saying that we call the angels who come down from God for the benefit of men some other kind of being; and he says that presumably we would call them demons. He does not see that the name “demons” is not even neutral, as the name “men” is, among whom some are good and some bad. Nor is it a good name, as the name “gods” is, which is applied, not to base things, whether demons or statues or animals, but, by those who know the things of God, to beings that are truly more divine and blessed. The name “demons,” on the other hand, is always applied to the wicked powers that are outside the grosser body, which lead men astray and distract them and drag them down from God and from the things above the heavens to the affairs of this world.
translator_notes: Only λόγος carries quotation marks in Koetschau’s text; σοφία and ἀλήθεια are titles of Christ drawn from Scripture, cited as clear allusions: John 1:1 (Word), 1 Corinthians 1:24 (Christ the wisdom of God; Proverbs 8 also possible), John 14:6 (the truth). ‘Call upon’ (καλέσαι) means invoke in prayer, as the next sentence shows. ἄλλο τι γένος παρὰ θεοῦ: read παρὰ θεοῦ with καταβαίνοντας (‘who come down from God’); a reading ‘some kind other than a god’ is grammatically possible and would fit Celsus’s question ‘gods or some other kind’. ‘Purpose’ renders προαίρεσις (deliberate choice, will). ‘Statues’ renders ἀγάλματα (cult images). ‘Outside the grosser body’ (ἔξω τοῦ παχυτέρου σώματος): powers not clothed in the coarse body humans have; Origen does not say they are wholly bodiless. ‘Things above the heavens’ = τὰ ὑπερουράνια. No direct Scripture quotation beyond the titles of Christ.

title: Celsus misreads Jewish worship
english: After this he sets out a passage about the Jews, as follows: “First, then, one may well wonder at the Jews, that they revere heaven and the angels in it, yet pass over the most venerable and most powerful parts of it, the sun and the moon and the other stars, both fixed and wandering; as if it were possible for the whole to be a god while its parts are not divine. Or that they worship most devoutly beings who are said to draw near, somewhere in the dark, to people blinded by a crooked sorcery or dreaming through dim phantoms, while those who prophesy so plainly and so brilliantly to all, through whom rains and heat and clouds and thunders (which they worship) and lightnings and fruits and every kind of offspring are dispensed, through whom God is revealed to them, the most manifest heralds of the world above, the truly heavenly angels, these they count as nothing.”

In these remarks Celsus seems to me to be confused, and to have written, from things he heard amiss, about matters he did not know. For it is clear to those who examine the ways of the Jews and set those of the Christians beside them that the Jews follow the law, which says in the person of God: “You shall have no other gods besides me. You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor a likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is on the earth beneath, or that is in the waters under the earth. You shall not worship them, nor serve them” (Exodus 20:3–5). Following this law, they revere nothing but the God over all, who made heaven and everything else.

And it is plain that those who live by the law, revering the One who made heaven, do not revere heaven together with God; nor does anyone who serves the law of Moses worship the angels in heaven either. Just as they do not worship the sun and the moon and the stars, “the array of heaven,” so they abstain from worshipping heaven and the angels in it, obeying the law which says: “And do not, when you look up to heaven and see the sun and the moon and the stars, all the array of heaven, be led astray and worship them and serve them, things which the Lord your God has allotted to all the nations” (Deuteronomy 4:19).
translator_notes: Celsus’s passage runs from πρῶτον οὖν to τὸ μηδέν; Origen’s reply begins at ἐν τούτοις δὲ δοκεῖ μοι. Celsus’s sentence changes construction midway (θαυμάζειν ἄξιον εἰ … then accusative-and-infinitive θρησκεύειν … ἡγεῖσθαι); rendered ‘Or that they …’ to keep his dependence on ‘one may well wonder’. ‘Which they worship’ refers grammatically to the thunders (ἃς … βροντάς), as Celsus has it. Exodus 20:3–5 (first half of v. 5) is quoted in LXX wording; the parallel Deuteronomy 5:7–9 is near identical. θεοὶ in Exodus 20:3 is a bracketed supplement in Koetschau’s text, followed (it is in the LXX). Deuteronomy 4:19 LXX quoted, ending before τοῖς ὑποκάτω τοῦ οὐρανοῦ. ‘Array of heaven’ renders LXX ὁ κόσμος τοῦ οὐρανοῦ (Hebrew ‘host of heaven’); ‘array’ keeps both order and adornment. ‘In the person of God’ = ἐκ προσώπου θεοῦ. ‘Fixed and wandering’ = ἀπλανεῖς τε καὶ πλανήτας. ‘Every kind of offspring’ renders γονὰς ἁπάσας (births, generation of living things).

title: A divine whole does not make its parts divine
english: Celsus also assumes, on his own account, that the Jews regard heaven as a god, and he adds to this something he presents as absurd. He accuses those who worship heaven but not also the sun, the moon and the stars, saying that the Jews do this “as if it were possible for the whole to be a god while its parts are not divine.” By the whole he seems to mean heaven, and by its parts the sun, the moon and the stars.

Now neither Jews nor Christians plainly say that heaven is a god. But let it be granted, on his terms, that the Jews say heaven is a god, and let the sun, the moon and the stars also be parts of heaven (which is not necessarily true, for the animals and plants on earth are not parts of the earth either). On what ground is it true, even by the Greeks’ own account, that if some whole is a god, its parts are thereby divine as well? The Greeks plainly say that the whole world is a god: the Stoics say it is the first god, the followers of Plato the second, and some of them the third. Do such men hold, then, that since the world as a whole is a god, its parts too are thereby divine, so that not only human beings but also all the irrational animals are divine, being parts of the world, and the plants as well? And if the mountains, the rivers and the seas are parts of the world, are the rivers and the seas therefore gods because the whole world is a god? But the Greeks will not say this either. Rather, it is the demons (or gods, as they name them) that preside over rivers and seas, if there are any, that they would call gods.

And so Celsus’s general rule proves false even by the account of those Greeks who bring in providence: the rule that if some whole is a god, its parts are necessarily divine. It follows from Celsus’s argument that if the world is a god, everything in it is divine, being a part of the world. On that reasoning, flies, gnats, worms and every kind of snake, and of birds and fishes too, will be divine living beings; and not even those who say that the world is a god will say that. But the Jews who live by the law of Moses, even if they do not know at all how to understand the meaning of the law, which is expressed in a hidden way and points to something secret, will say neither that heaven is a god nor that the angels are.
translator_notes: Celsus's phrase from 5.6 (ὡς ἐνδεχόμενον τὸ μὲν ὅλον εἶναι θεόν, τὰ μέρη δ᾿ αὐτοῦ μὴ θεῖα) is set in quotation marks, in the same English used for Celsus's quotation in 5.6; the rest of the opening is Origen's report of Celsus's view. ἑαυτῷ λαβών rendered 'assumes, on his own account'; τούτῳ ὡς ἄτοπον ἐπιφέρει 'adds to this something he presents as absurd'. '(θεόν)' is an editorial supplement in the staged text, adopted from 5.6. θεός here is the pagan philosophical notion of a cosmic god, so rendered lowercase 'a god' throughout (not the God of Scripture). σαφῶς in 'οὐ λέγουσι μὲν οὖν σαφῶς' rendered 'plainly'; it qualifies the saying (they do not plainly say it), not an assertion that it is clear, and it answers the later σαφῶς of the Greeks who 'plainly say' the world is a god. Stoics/Platonists: 'the first god ... the second ... some of them the third' follows the Greek exactly; τινὲς δ᾿ αὐτῶν most naturally means some of the Platonists, left as 'some of them'. ἤδη ('already', i.e. by that fact) rendered 'thereby'; πάντως 'necessarily' in both places. δαίμονας rendered 'demons' (consistent with the rest of this translation), with Origen's own gloss 'or gods, as they name them'; εἰ ἄρα rendered 'if there are any'. The staged text has stray full stops before ψεῦδος and πάντως and after ἆρ᾿ οὖν κατὰ τοὺς τοιούτους; punctuation regularised by sense. No Scripture quoted.

title: Worshipping heaven and angels breaks the Jewish law
english: Since we say that he was confused by certain things he misheard, come, let us for our part make these points clear too, as far as we can, and show that, though Celsus thinks it a Jewish practice to worship heaven and the angels in it, such a practice is not Jewish but a transgression of Judaism, as is the worship of the sun, the moon and the stars, and of images too. You will find, at any rate, especially in Jeremiah, the word of God reproaching the Jewish people through the prophet for worshipping such things and for sacrificing “to the queen of heaven” (Jeremiah 44:17–19) and “to all the host of heaven” (Jeremiah 19:13).

The writings of the Christians also show, when they denounce the sins committed among the Jews, that once God had abandoned that people for certain sins, they committed these sins as well. For in the Acts of the Apostles it is written about the Jews: “But God turned and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: Did you offer me slain beasts and sacrifices forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? And you took up the tent of Moloch and the star of the god Rompha, the figures which you made in order to worship them” (Acts 7:42–43; Amos 5:25–26).

And in Paul, who was strictly trained in the ways of the Jews (Acts 22:3) and later became a Christian through an extraordinary appearance of Jesus (Acts 9:3–6), such things are said in the letter to the Colossians: “Let no one disqualify you, insisting on humility and the worship of angels, dwelling on what he has seen, puffed up without cause by the mind of his flesh, and not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body, supplied and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with the growth that is from God” (Colossians 2:18–19).
But Celsus, having neither read nor learned these things, has represented the Jews, I do not know how, as worshipping heaven and the angels in it without breaking the law.
translator_notes: Jeremiah: 'the queen of heaven' (τῇ βασιλίσσῃ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ) is LXX Jeremiah 51:17-19, which is English Jeremiah 44:17-19 (also 44:25; at Jeremiah 7:18 the LXX reads 'the host of heaven' instead of 'the queen of heaven'). 'To all the host of heaven' (πάσῃ τῇ στρατιᾷ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ) matches Jeremiah 19:13 (cf. 8:2); chapter numbering in Jeremiah 19 is the same in LXX and English. Acts 7:42-43 quotes Amos 5:25-26 LXX; Origen's text reads the god's name as Ῥομφᾶ (NA: Ῥαιφάν, 'Rephan'), kept as 'Rompha'. Koetschau punctuates the whole quotation as one question; the question mark is placed after 'O house of Israel' as in the biblical text, without change of sense. 'Strictly trained in the ways of the Jews' is a clear echo of Acts 22:3 (πεπαιδευμένος κατὰ ἀκρίβειαν); 'an extraordinary appearance of Jesus' (ἐκ παραδόξου ἐπιφανείας) refers to the Damascus road (Acts 9:3-6). Colossians 2:18 θέλων ἐν ταπεινοφροσύνῃ is the Septuagintal idiom 'delighting in / insisting on'; ἃ ἑώρακεν ἐμβατεύων rendered 'dwelling on what he has seen'. τὴν αὔξησιν τοῦ θεοῦ rendered 'the growth that is from God'. ἀγάλμασιν rendered 'images'. φέρε kept as 'come'; ἡμεῖς and καὶ ταῦτα as 'for our part' and 'these points too'.

title: Sorcery and star-worship are both against the law
english: Further, being somewhat confused, and not having looked carefully into what concerns this subject, he supposed that the Jews were led on by the spells used in magic and sorcery to worship the angels in heaven, because of certain phantoms that appear, in answer to the spells, to those who chant them. He did not see that this too, in those who did such things, was done against the law, which says: “You shall not follow mediums, and you shall not attach yourselves to enchanters, so as to be defiled by them: I am the Lord your God” (Leviticus 19:31).

He ought, then, since he regards the Jews as keeping the law and says that they are the ones who live by the law, either not to have attributed these things to the Jews at all, or, if he attributed them, to have shown that it was the Jews who broke the law who did such things. But again: just as those break the law who, blinded and dreaming through dim phantoms, worship by sorcery beings somewhere in the dark, bowing down to those said to draw near and to others of that kind, so too those who sacrifice to the sun, the moon and the stars break the law most thoroughly. And it was not consistent for the same man to say that the Jews are on their guard against worshipping the sun, the moon and the stars, and yet are not on their guard against such worship where heaven and angels are concerned.
translator_notes: Leviticus 19:31 is quoted from the LXX (οὐκ ἐπακολουθήσετε ἐγγαστριμύθοις ... ἐγώ εἰμι κύριος ὁ θεὸς ὑμῶν; Origen's text lacks εἰμι). ἐγγαστρίμυθοι ('those who speak from the belly') rendered 'mediums'. μαγγανεῖαι rendered 'magic' (Origen's usual sense: magical arts), alongside γοητεῖαι 'sorcery'. In the second paragraph Origen reuses Celsus's own words from 5.6 (ἐν σκότῳ που, ἐκ γοητείας, τυφλώττουσιν, δι᾿ ἀμυδρῶν φασμάτων ὀνειρώττουσιν, ἐγχρίμπτειν λεγομένους, εὖ μάλα) and turns Celsus's 'they worship most devoutly' (εὖ μάλα θρησκεύειν) into 'they break the law most thoroughly' (εὖ μάλα παρανομοῦσι); the echoed phrases are not set in quotation marks because Origen recasts their syntax, and the English reuses the 5.6 wording ('somewhere in the dark', 'blinded', 'dreaming through dim phantoms', 'said to draw near'). The dative καὶ τοῖς τοιούτοις after προσκυνοῦντες is loose; rendered 'and to others of that kind'. ὑποσυγκεχυμένος is 'somewhat confused' (ὑπο- softens); ἔτι is 'further', not 'still more'. τὸν τηροῦντα rendered 'since he regards'. The final sentence is elliptical (οὐκ ἦν κατὰ τὸν αὐτόν, 'it was not for the same man'), rendered 'it was not consistent for the same man'.

title: God’s people are to shine like the stars, not worship them
english: But if we, who refuse to worship angels and the sun, the moon and the stars alike, must make a defence for not worshipping even those whom the Greeks call visible and perceptible gods, we will say that the law of Moses also knows that these were allotted by God “to all the nations under heaven” (Deuteronomy 4:19), but not to those who were taken as God’s chosen portion out of all the nations on earth. It is written, at any rate, in Deuteronomy: “And do not, when you look up to heaven and see the sun and the moon and the stars, all the array of heaven, be led astray and worship them and serve them, things which the Lord your God allotted to all the nations under the whole heaven. But the Lord God took us and brought us out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt, to be a people of his own inheritance, as on this day” (Deuteronomy 4:19–20).

So then the Hebrew people, called by God to be “a chosen race” and “a royal priesthood” and “a holy nation” and “a people for his possession” (1 Peter 2:9; Exodus 19:6), the people about whom it had been foretold to Abraham by the voice of the Lord speaking to him, “Look up to heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them. And he said to him: So shall your offspring be” (Genesis 15:5), this people, having the hope of becoming like the stars in heaven, was not going to worship those whom they were to resemble through understanding and keeping the law of God. For it has been said to them: “The Lord your God has multiplied you, and behold, you are today like the stars of heaven in number” (Deuteronomy 1:10). And in Daniel also such things are prophesied about the resurrection: “And at that time your people shall be saved, everyone who is written in the book; and many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to reproach and everlasting shame; and those who understand shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and from among the many righteous, like the stars, for ever and beyond” (Daniel 12:1–3). From this Paul too takes his point when, speaking of the resurrection, he says: “There are also heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; but the glory of the heavenly is one, and the glory of the earthly is another. There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15:40–42).

It was not reasonable, then, that those who had been taught to rise with greatness of soul above all created things, and to hope from God for the best things for themselves in return for the noblest life; who had heard the words “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14) and “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16); who train themselves to possess Wisdom, “bright and unfading” (Wisdom of Solomon 6:12), or have already received that Wisdom, which is “the radiance of eternal light” (Wisdom of Solomon 7:26), should be so struck with awe at the perceptible light of the sun and the moon and the stars that, because of that perceptible light of theirs, they should think themselves somewhere beneath them, though they possess so great an intelligible light of knowledge, and “the true light” (John 1:9), and “the light of the world” (John 8:12), and “the light of men” (John 1:4), and that they should worship those bodies.

If those bodies ought to be worshipped at all, they ought to be worshipped not for the perceptible light admired by the many but for their intelligible and true light, if indeed the stars in heaven are also rational and virtuous living beings and have been enlightened with the light of knowledge by Wisdom, which is “the radiance of eternal light” (Wisdom of Solomon 7:26). For their perceptible light is the work of the Creator of all things, while their intelligible light is perhaps also their own, having come from the free will within them.
translator_notes: Deuteronomy 4:19-20 is quoted from the LXX; Origen's text reads ἡμᾶς ('us') where the LXX has ὑμᾶς ('you'), kept as 'us'; κόσμος τοῦ οὐρανοῦ rendered 'the array of heaven'; ἔγκληρον 'of his own inheritance'; καὶ μή ποτε ... προσκυνήσῃς rendered as a prohibition ('And do not ... be led astray and worship them'), as in the 5.6 English of Deuteronomy 4:19. ἐπ᾿ ἴσης μὴ προσκυνοῦντας rendered 'who refuse to worship angels and the sun, the moon and the stars alike'. The four titles (γένος ἐκλεκτόν, βασίλειον ἱεράτευμα, ἔθνος ἅγιον, λαὸς εἰς περιποίησιν) match 1 Peter 2:9 word for word, which itself draws on Exodus 19:6 and Isaiah 43:20-21; Exodus 19:6 cited as the source of 'royal priesthood' and 'holy nation'. Uncited possible allusion: 'chosen portion out of all the nations on earth' may echo Deuteronomy 32:9 / 7:6 / 14:2 (μερίς, ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν ἐθνῶν); left in this note as uncertain. Deuteronomy 1:10 matches the LXX wording exactly (Deuteronomy 10:22 is similar but differs). Daniel 12:1-3 follows the Theodotion Greek ('and from the many righteous like the stars for ever and beyond'). In the sentence beginning 'So then the Hebrew people', the subject is singular λαός with a plural participle κληθέντες; English keeps 'people' and resumes it ('this people') after the Genesis quotation for clarity. περὶ αὐτῶν in 'to hope for the best things' read as reflexive (αὑτῶν, 'for themselves'). Wisdom of Solomon 6:12 (λαμπρὰ καὶ ἀμάραντός ἐστιν ἡ σοφία) is a clear verbal allusion; ἀπαύγασμα φωτὸς ἀϊδίου is Wisdom of Solomon 7:26 (also echoed at Hebrews 1:3, 'radiance of his glory', not cited). Wisdom is capitalised because Origen identifies it as 'the radiance of eternal light', his title for the Son. 'The light of the world' in the list of titles is cited to John 8:12 (the Son's self-description), distinct from the disciples' 'light of the world' at Matthew 5:14 a few lines earlier. σπουδαῖα rendered 'virtuous' (morally excellent, the philosophical sense). Origen's view that the stars are rational living beings is stated conditionally (εἴπερ, 'if indeed'), and the intelligible light's source in their free will is qualified by τάχα ('perhaps'); both kept. The second paragraph of the closing argument translates οὓς εἰ ἄρα προσκυνεῖσθαι ἐχρῆν, which grammatically continues the long sentence; split for readability without change of sense.

title: Not even the sun asks to be worshipped
english: But not even that light of theirs should be worshipped by one who sees and understands the true light, by sharing in which these too, it seems, have been given light; nor by one who sees God, the Father of the true light. Of him it is well said: “God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5).

Those who worship the sun, the moon and the stars because their light is visible and heavenly would not worship a spark of fire or a lamp on earth, for they see how beyond comparison the things they think worthy of worship surpass the light of sparks and lamps. In the same way, those who have understood in what sense “God is light” (1 John 1:5), who have grasped in what sense the Son of God is “the true light, which enlightens every man coming into the world” (John 1:9), and who understand too in what sense he says, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), could not reasonably worship what is, so to speak, a tiny spark of true light in the sun, the moon and the stars, set beside the light that God is.

Nor do we say such things about the sun, the moon and the stars because we despise these great works of God, or because we call the sun, the moon and the stars “a red-hot mass”, as Anaxagoras did. We say them because we perceive the divinity of God, whose pre-eminence is beyond words, and also how his Only-begotten surpasses all the rest. And since we are persuaded that the sun itself, and the moon and the stars, pray to the God who is over all through his Only-begotten, we judge that we ought not to pray to those who are themselves praying. For they themselves wish to send us up to the God to whom they pray, rather than draw us down to themselves, or split our power of prayer, turning part of it away from God and toward themselves.

Here I will also use the following example about them. Our Saviour and Lord, hearing himself once addressed as “Good Teacher” (Mark 10:17; Luke 18:18), sent the speaker back to his own Father and said: “Why do you call me good? No one is good but one, God the Father” (Mark 10:18; Luke 18:19). If the Son of the Father’s “love” (Colossians 1:13), being the “image” of God’s goodness (Wisdom of Solomon 7:26), had good reason to say this, how much more reason would the sun have to say to those who worship it: “Why do you worship me? For ‘you shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve’ (Matthew 4:10; Deuteronomy 6:13); and him I too, and all who are with me, worship and serve.”

And even if someone is not so great, let such a one none the less pray to the Word of God, who is able to heal him, and much more to his Father, who for the righteous of earlier times also “sent forth his word and healed them, and delivered them from their destruction” (Psalm 107:20).
translator_notes: Opening αὐτό (neuter) taken as the stars' intelligible light from the end of 5.10, hence 'that light of theirs'. The phrase τὸν οἱονεὶ βραχὺν σπινθῆρα ὡς πρὸς φῶς τὸν θεὸν ἀληθινοῦ φωτός is syntactically loose; read as 'a tiny spark of true light ... compared with the light, God'; an alternative takes ἀληθινοῦ φωτός with τὸν θεόν ('God of true light'). The full stop the source prints before ἢ κατάγειν is read as a comparative (rather ... than). Anaxagoras' 'red-hot mass' (μύδρος διάπυρος) is a doxographic report (cf. Diogenes Laertius 2.8), not a quotation, so no inline source given. Mark 10:18 / Luke 18:19 quoted with Origen's addition 'the Father'. Matthew 4:10 wording; it adapts Deuteronomy 6:13 LXX (which has 'fear'). Psalm 106:20 LXX = Psalm 107:20 English. 'Only-begotten' is a title (John 1:14, 18), left uncited. 'Image of his goodness' = Wisdom of Solomon 7:26 (same verse as 'radiance of eternal light' in 5.10).

title: God is near; the stars are only his heralds
english: God, then, in his kindness comes down to men, not in a spatial sense but by his providence. And the Child of God is with his own disciples not only at that time but always, fulfilling the words, “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). And if “a branch cannot bear fruit unless it abides in the vine” (John 15:4), it is clear that the disciples of the Word as well, the spiritual “branches” (John 15:5) of the true vine, the Word (John 15:1), cannot bear the fruits of virtue unless they remain in the true vine, the Christ of God. He is with us too, whose place is here below on earth; and being with those everywhere who have grown into him, and indeed with those who do not know him, he is everywhere. John, who wrote the Gospel, shows this too in the person of John the Baptist, who says: “Among you stands one whom you do not know, who comes after me” (John 1:26–27).

Since he who has filled heaven and earth, and has said, “Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord” (Jeremiah 23:24), is with us and is near us (for I believe him when he says, “I am a God at hand, and not a God far off, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 23:23)), it is absurd to seek to pray to the sun or the moon or any of the stars, which do not reach to all things.

But let it be granted, to use Celsus’s very words, that the sun, the moon and the stars are “prophesying rains and heat and clouds and thunder”. If, then, they prophesy such great things, should we not rather worship God, in whose service they prophesy, and revere him rather than his prophets? Let them, then, prophesy “lightnings, too, and fruits and every kind of offspring”, and let them “dispense” all such things; yet we will not for that reason worship those who themselves worship, just as we do not worship Moses either, or those after him who prophesied from God things better than rain and heat and clouds and thunder and lightning and fruits and every offspring the senses perceive. But even if the sun, the moon and the stars were able to utter prophecies better than rains, not even so will we worship them, but the Father of the prophecies in them, and the Word of God, who is the minister of those prophecies.
But grant that they are also his “heralds” and “truly heavenly angels”. Even so, how should we not worship the God whom they herald and announce, rather than his heralds and his angels?
translator_notes: ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ παῖς rendered 'the Child of God' (the title of Acts 4:27, 30; possible allusion, left uncited). 'Not only at that time' = during his earthly life. The marked phrases 'prophesying rains and heat and clouds and thunder', 'lightnings, too, and fruits and every kind of offspring', 'dispense', 'heralds' and 'truly heavenly angels' are Celsus's own words from his passage quoted in 5.6. ἀγγέλους / ἀγγελλόμενον is a wordplay (angels / announced) that English cannot keep fully. Jeremiah 23:23 LXX is a statement ('I am a God at hand'), whereas the Hebrew is a question; LXX and English verse numbers agree in Jeremiah 23. The closing clause (τὸν διάκονον αὐτῶν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ) is rendered 'the Word of God, who serves him in them'; literally 'their minister, the Word of God'. The 'true vine' (John 15:1) and 'branches' (John 15:5) are cited as allusions. νοητά ('intelligible', grasped by the mind) is rendered 'spiritual' for readability; it is not πνευματικός.

title: The stars await the freedom of God’s children
english: Celsus takes it for granted that we hold the sun, the moon and the stars to be “nothing”. About them we confess that they too wait for “the revelation of the sons of God” (Romans 8:19), being subjected for the present to “the futility” of material bodies “because of him who subjected them in hope” (Romans 8:20).

If Celsus had read the countless other things we say about the sun, the moon and the stars, and the words “Praise him, all you stars and light” (Psalm 148:3) and “Praise him, you heavens of heavens” (Psalm 148:4), he would not have declared of us that we say these great beings, which praise God greatly, are “nothing”. Nor does Celsus know the words: “For the eager longing of the creation waits for the revelation of the sons of God. For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope that the creation itself also will be set free from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Romans 8:19–21).

With this, then, let our defence for not revering the sun, the moon and the stars come to an end. Let us also set out his next passage, so that afterwards, God granting, we may say in reply to it whatever will be given us from the light of the truth.
translator_notes: 'Nothing' (τὸ μηδέν) is Celsus's word from his passage in 5.6, so it is quoted. In the first allusion to Romans 8:20 Origen inserts 'of material bodies' between the quoted words and applies the passage to the heavenly bodies; the plural ('them') follows his adaptation. Psalm 148:3–4: LXX and English numbering agree; the LXX 'all the stars and the light' differs from the Hebrew 'all you stars of light'. Origen's view that the stars are living, rational beings (cf. 5.10) is kept as he states it.

title: Celsus mocks the hope of the resurrection
english: He says, then: “It is foolish of them also to think that when God, like a cook, brings on the fire, all the rest of the race will be roasted through, while they alone will survive, not only the living but also those who died long ago, rising up from the earth in that very same flesh. This is simply the hope of worms. For what human soul would still long for a body that has rotted? Seeing that this doctrine is not shared even by some among you and among the Christians, one may show how utterly foul and loathsome it is, and at the same time impossible. For what body, once wholly corrupted, can return to its original nature, and to that very first make-up from which it was dissolved? Having nothing to answer, they flee to a most absurd refuge: that everything is possible to God (Matthew 19:26). But God cannot do what is shameful, nor does he will what is against nature. Nor, if you in your own depravity desire something vile, will God be able to do it, nor need one believe at once that it will happen. For God is the author not of faulty appetite, nor of wandering disorder, but of right and just nature. He could grant everlasting life to a soul; but ‘corpses’, says Heraclitus, ‘are more fit to be thrown out than dung’ (Heraclitus, fragment 96). As for flesh, full of things it is not even decent to name, God will neither wish nor be able to make it everlasting against reason. For he himself is the reason of all things that exist; he can therefore do nothing contrary to reason, nor contrary to himself.”
translator_notes: The whole chapter is Celsus's text, quoted by Origen, so it stands in one quotation. ὁπότε μηδ᾿ ὑμῶν τοῦτο τὸ δόγμα καὶ τῶν Χριστιανῶν ἐνίοις κοινόν ἐστι: Rendered 'some among you and among the Christians' to keep the Greek open: καί may join two groups ('you' = the Jews, whom Celsus addresses with the Christians from 5.2) or be explanatory ('some of you, that is, of the Christians'). Reviewer changed the earlier explanatory rendering, which settled the question the Greek leaves open. The infinitive ἀποφαίνειν has no governing verb in the transmitted text (perhaps a corruption); rendered 'one may show'. 'Everything is possible to God' echoes Matthew 19:26 (also Mark 10:27) and is cited though Celsus says it. Heraclitus = Diels-Kranz 22 B96. λόγος is lower-case 'reason' here because it is Celsus's philosophical sense, with his play on παραλόγως / παράλογον ('against reason'). γένος rendered 'race' (Celsus means the rest of mankind).

title: The fire that cleanses and heals
english: See, then, how here, from the very start, he slanders with mockery the burning of the world, a teaching put forward also by some Greeks whose philosophy is not to be despised, and how he would have it that we, as though making God a cook, bring in our account of that burning. He has not seen that, as some Greeks held (perhaps having taken it from the most ancient nation, the Hebrews), the fire is brought upon the world to cleanse it, and probably also upon each of those who need the punishment and at the same time the healing that comes through fire. It burns, but does not burn up, those who have no matter that needs to be consumed by that fire; but it burns and burns up those who, in the building that is spoken of figuratively, the building of deeds, words and thoughts, have built with “wood, hay or straw” (1 Corinthians 3:12).

The divine words say that the Lord will come “like a refiner’s fire and like fullers’ soap” (Malachi 3:2) to each of those who need it, because there has been mixed into them, as it were, a base matter that melts, the matter that comes from wickedness; to those, I mean, who need fire, as though he were smelting those who have been mixed with “bronze and tin and lead” (Ezekiel 22:18–20). Anyone who wishes may learn this from the prophet Ezekiel.

That we do not say God brings the fire like a cook, but as God, the benefactor of those who need pain and fire, the prophet Isaiah will also bear witness, in the place where it is written that it was said to a certain sinful nation: “Since you have coals of fire, sit upon them; these will be a help to you” (Isaiah 47:14–15). The Word, arranging what suits the multitudes who will read Scripture, speaks the grim things in a veiled way and with wisdom, to bring fear on those who cannot otherwise turn back from the flood of their sins. Even so, the attentive reader will find shown there the end that the grim and painful things bring about for those who suffer. For the present it is enough to set down these words from Isaiah: “For my name’s sake I will show you my anger, and I will bring my glories upon you, so that I may not utterly destroy you” (Isaiah 48:9).

We have been compelled to hint at things that do not suit those who believe more simply and who need a simpler handling in our teaching, so as not to seem to leave unrefuted the charge Celsus makes when he says, “when God, like a cook, brings on the fire.”
translator_notes: ἐκπύρωσις = the Stoic doctrine of the world's periodic conflagration, rendered 'the burning of the world'. The source prints ῾Πσαΐας, a misprint for Ἡσαΐας (Isaiah). ὡς ποίαν πλυνόντων: the LXX of Malachi 3:2 has πόα ('fullers' herb', i.e. soap). The Ezekiel reference is to the smelting of Israel mixed with bronze, tin and lead (Ezekiel 22:18–20 LXX; LXX lists bronze, iron, tin, lead); same numbering in English. Isaiah 47:14–15 follows the LXX, which has the coals as a help; the Hebrew says there is no coal to warm oneself by. Isaiah 48:9 LXX ('I will bring my glories upon you') differs from the Hebrew ('for my praise I restrain it for you'). χύσις τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων ('outpouring of sins') rendered 'flood of their sins'. The closing quotation repeats Celsus's words from 5.14. Isaiah 47:14-15: in Rahlfs the coals clause ends 47:14 and 'these will be a help to you' opens 47:15.

title: Simple believers and the fire of punishment
english: From what has been said it is clear, to those who listen with more understanding, how one must answer also his words, “all the rest of the race will be roasted through, while they alone will survive.” It is no wonder if such ideas have been formed by those among us whom the Word calls “the foolish things of the world”, “the low-born”, “the despised” and “the things that are not” (1 Corinthians 1:27–28), those whom “through the foolishness of preaching God was pleased to save”, namely “those who believe” in him, “since in the wisdom of God the world through wisdom did not know God” (1 Corinthians 1:21). They are not able to set out clearly the sense of the passages, nor have they been willing to give their time to searching the Scripture, although Jesus says, “Search the Scriptures” (John 5:39); and so they have formed such notions about the fire that God brings on and about what will happen to those who have sinned.

And perhaps, just as it suits children to be told certain things fitted to their infancy, so as to turn them, being very young children, toward what is better, so for those whom the Word has named the foolish things of the world, the low-born and the despised, the obvious understanding of the punishments is fitting, since they can take in no other way of turning back and of keeping away from their many evils than through fear and the imagining of the punishments.

The Word, then, says that only those will survive without a taste of the fire and the punishments who have been perfectly purified in their doctrines, their character and the ruling part of their soul. But those who are not such, who according to their deserts need the dispensation of punishment through fire, it says will be in these punishments for some end; an end which it befits God to bring upon those who were made “in his image” (Genesis 1:26–27) and have lived against the purpose of the nature that is “in his image.” This, too, is our answer to the words, “all the rest of the race will be roasted through, while they alone will survive.”
translator_notes: The subject of νενόηκε and ὑπείληφε is the neuter plural 'the foolish things' among us (simple believers), not Celsus; the neuter participles that follow agree with them. 1 Corinthians 1:21 is quoted with its clauses reordered and with 'in him' (αὐτῷ) added; the relative ἅτινα makes the syntax loose, smoothed here with 'namely'. ἐξουδενωμένα is Origen's spelling for the ἐξουθενημένα of 1 Corinthians 1:28. ἡγεμονικόν (the Stoic 'ruling faculty') rendered 'the ruling part of their soul'. ἐπί τινι τέλει rendered 'for some end', without deciding whether it means a purpose or a time limit. 'In his image' = Genesis 1:26–27 (κατ᾿ εἰκόνα), cited once. The quoted phrase at the opening and close repeats Celsus's words from 5.14. διαμενεῖν is rendered 'survive' both in Celsus's phrase and in Origen's answer, since Origen turns Celsus's own verb back on him.

title: Paul counts himself among the living
english: Next, having misunderstood either the sacred writings or those who have not understood the sacred writings, he says that we teach that at the time of the cleansing that will be brought upon the world through fire, we alone will survive, “not only those then living but also those who died long ago.” He did not grasp that it was with a certain secret wisdom that the apostle of Jesus said: “We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet; for the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:51–52). He ought to have considered what the speaker had in mind when, as one by no means dead, he set himself and those like him apart from the dead, and after “and the dead will be raised incorruptible” said: “and we shall be changed.”

To confirm that the apostle had some such meaning when he wrote the words I have quoted from the First Letter to the Corinthians, I will quote also the words from the First Letter to the Thessalonians, where Paul, as one living and awake and other than those who have fallen asleep, says this: “For this we say to you by the word of the Lord, that we who are living, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will by no means go before those who have fallen asleep; for the Lord himself will come down from heaven with a word of command, with the voice of an archangel and with the trumpet of God” (1 Thessalonians 4:15–16). Then again, right after this, knowing that the dead in Christ are others than himself and those like him, he goes on to say: “The dead in Christ will rise first; then we who are living, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air” (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17).
translator_notes: Celsus is reported in indirect speech; Origen's μόνους διαμενεῖν (without Celsus's αὐτούς) is rendered as his paraphrase 'we alone will survive', unquoted; the phrase οὐ μόνον τοὺς ζῶντας τότε ἀλλὰ καὶ τοὺς πάλαι ποτὲ ἀποθανόντας repeats Celsus's words at 5.14 and is quoted in the same English wording used there ('not only those then living but also those who died long ago'). Reviewer: rendered τοῦ ἐπαχθησομένου ... διὰ πυρός as 'brought upon the world through fire' (fire is the means, not the agent). καθαρσίου is taken as the noun 'cleansing' (purification), governed by τοῦ ἐπαχθησομένου. σαλπίσει γάρ is impersonal in Greek ('it will sound'); rendered 'the trumpet will sound'. The staged text has a full stop after γεγραφέναι, which breaks one sentence; the translation reads εἰς βεβαίωσιν ... γεγραφέναι ἃ παρεθέμην ... παραθήσομαι as one sentence. ἐν κελεύσματι rendered 'with a word of command'.

title: The seed and the body that is to be
english: He has mocked at some length the resurrection of the flesh, which is preached in the churches but understood more clearly by the wiser. There is no need to set out his words again, since they have already been quoted once. Come, then, let us set out and present a few things on this problem too, as far as we can, with an eye to those who will read this, as befits a defence addressed to one who is a stranger to the faith and written for the sake of those who are still infants, tossed by waves and carried about “by every wind of doctrine, by the trickery of men, in craftiness, toward the scheming of error” (Ephesians 4:14).

Neither we nor the divine writings say that those who died long ago will live, “rising up from the earth” in the very same flesh, flesh that has received no change for the better; Celsus slanders us in saying so. For we hear many scriptures speaking of the resurrection in a way worthy of God, but for the present it is enough to quote Paul’s words from the First Letter to the Corinthians, where he says: “But someone will say, ‘How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?’ Foolish one! What you sow is not made alive unless it dies. And what you sow, you do not sow the body that is to be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of some other kind; but God gives it a body as he willed, and to each of the seeds its own body” (1 Corinthians 15:35–38).

See how in these words he says that it is “not the body that is to be” that is sown, but that from what is sown and cast bare upon the earth, as God gives “to each of the seeds its own body,” a kind of resurrection takes place, as a stalk rises from the seed cast down in plants such as mustard, or, in the case of a larger tree, from the stone of an olive or of some fruit tree.
translator_notes: The quoted phrase “rising up from the earth” repeats Celsus's wording at 5.14 (ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ἀναδύντας) in the English used there; αὐταῖς σαρξί (Origen drops Celsus's ἐκείναις) is left unquoted as 'in the very same flesh'. στάχυς rendered 'stalk' here and at 5.22, since Origen applies it to mustard as well as grain. The opening Greek sentence (Ἐπεὶ ... φέρε ... ἐκθώμεθα) is split into three English sentences; the staged text's full stops after νενοημένην and μεθοδίαν τῆς πλάνης are editorial and break one period. Ephesians 4:14: Origen's text adds ἐν πανουργίᾳ in parentheses as in Koetschau; κυβεία ('dice-play') rendered 'trickery'. Staged text has the typo σπερίρεις for σπείρεις; read σπείρεις. In 1 Corinthians 15:37 τῶν λοιπῶν rendered 'some other kind'. The mustard example may echo the parable of the mustard seed (Matthew 13:31–32), but Origen does not quote it; left uncited. ἀκρόδρυα = fruit trees with hard-shelled fruit (nuts and the like); rendered 'fruit tree'. 'in plants of this sort' renders ἐν τοῖς τοιοῖσδε (that is, grain such as wheat).

title: Sown a natural body, raised a spiritual body
english: So “God gives” “to each” “a body as he willed” (1 Corinthians 15:38): as with things that are sown, so also with those who are, as it were, sown in dying, and who at the fitting time receive from what was sown the “body” that God puts around each one according to his worth. We hear Scripture too, teaching at more length the difference between what is, so to speak, sown and what is, so to speak, raised from it, when it says: “It is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption; it is sown in dishonour, it is raised in glory; it is sown in weakness, it is raised in power; it is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body” (1 Corinthians 15:42–44).

Let anyone who is able go further and grasp what is meant by the one who says: “As is the one of dust, so are those who are of dust; and as is the heavenly one, so are those who are heavenly. And as we have borne the image of the one of dust, so let us also bear the image of the heavenly one” (1 Corinthians 15:48–49).

Though the apostle wished to hide the secret things of this passage, things that do not suit the simpler sort and the common hearing of those who are led to better things through believing, he was still compelled afterwards, so that we would not mishear his words, to say after “let us bear the image of the heavenly one” this: “This I say, brothers, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does corruption inherit incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15:50). Then, knowing something secret and mystical in the passage, as befitted one who was leaving his thoughts in writing for those who would come after him, he goes on to say: “Behold, I tell you a mystery” (1 Corinthians 15:51). This is the phrase usually set before things that are deeper and more mystical and are rightly hidden from the many; as it is written in Tobit: “It is good to hide a king’s mystery” (Tobit 12:7), while, with regard to what is glorious and suited to the many, together with truth given by way of accommodation, “it is good” “to reveal the works of God gloriously” (Tobit 12:7).

Our hope, then, is not the hope of worms, nor does our soul long for the body that has rotted. Even if the soul needs a body for moving from place to place, the soul that has meditated on “wisdom,” according to the words “The mouth of the righteous will meditate on wisdom” (Psalm 37:30), understands the difference between the earthly house that is being dissolved, in which the tent is, and the tent in which the righteous, “those who are” in it, groan, “being burdened,” not wishing to put off the tent but to “be clothed over” it, so that through this being “clothed over” “what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (2 Corinthians 5:1–4).

“For,” since every bodily nature is corruptible, “this corruptible” tent “must put on incorruption,” and its other aspect, which is “mortal” and liable to the death that follows on sin, must “put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53); so that when “the corruptible puts on incorruption and the mortal immortality, then” there “will come to pass” (1 Corinthians 15:54) what the prophets foretold long ago: the overthrow of the victory death won when it conquered us and made us subject to itself (Isaiah 25:8), and of the sting that comes from it, with which it stings the soul that is not guarded on every side and inflicts on it the wounds that come from sin (Hosea 13:14; 1 Corinthians 15:55–56).
translator_notes: LXX renumbering: 'The mouth of the righteous will meditate on wisdom' is LXX Psalm 36:30 = English Psalm 37:30 (LXX μελετήσει; Hebrew 'utters'); μελετάω kept as 'meditate' in both clauses to hold Origen's link. 'Not the hope of worms' and 'long for the body that has rotted' echo Celsus's words at 5.14 (σκωλήκων ἡ ἐλπίς; ποθήσειεν ἔτι σῶμα σεσηπός) but are not marked as a quotation in Origen's sentence, so they are left without quotation marks. σῶμα ψυχικόν rendered 'natural body' (literally 'soul-body', the body animated by soul); χοϊκός/ἐπουράνιος rendered 'the one of dust' / 'the heavenly one' without adding 'man'. 1 Corinthians 15:49: Origen reads the subjunctive φορέσωμεν ('let us bear'), a known variant, kept. ἀπόρρητα 'secret things'; ἁπλουστέροις rendered 'simpler believers' (the following clause names them as believers). The clause ὡς ἔπρεπε διὰ γραμμάτων καταλιπόντι τοῖς μετ᾿ αὐτὸν τὰ νενοημένα εἰρημένα is awkward in the staged text (εἰρημένα may be corrupt); rendered by sense. Tobit 12:7 (LXX; also 12:11) is quoted in two parts. οἰκονομικῶς ἀληθοῦς ('true by economy', truth adapted to the hearers' capacity in God's ordering of teaching) rendered 'truth given by way of accommodation'; doubtful nuance. 2 Corinthians 5:1–4: Origen reads ἀπεκδύσασθαι for ἐκδύσασθαι and distinguishes the 'earthly house' from the 'tent' (σκῆνος) inside it; τῷ σκήνει ἐπενδύσασθαι rendered 'be clothed over' the tent. τὸ ἕτερον αὐτοῦ ('the other [aspect] of it') rendered 'its other aspect'; Origen pairs corruptible/incorruption and mortal/immortality as two sides of the same tent. The prophecy of death's defeat is not quoted verbatim: Isaiah 25:8 (Paul's 'death is swallowed up in victory', not the LXX wording) and Hosea 13:14 ('where is your sting'), as joined in 1 Corinthians 15:54–56; cited as clear allusions. The staged text's full stop after προειρημένον stands for a colon (ἀναίρεσις is in apposition).

title: The Stoics’ Socrates born again
english: What we hold about the resurrection has now been said in part, as far as room allowed for the present; for we have composed a work on the resurrection elsewhere, where we examined the questions of this subject at greater length. Now we must deal, as is reasonable, with what Celsus says. He has neither understood what is written among us nor been able to judge that the meaning of those wise men must not be thought to be represented by people who profess nothing more than faith in the Christians’ teaching.

Come, let us show that men who are not to be despised for their logical theory and their dialectical inquiries have said things that are wholly absurd; and if any teachings are to be sneered at as base old wives’ tales, it is theirs rather than ours.

The Stoics say that periodically a conflagration of the universe takes place, and after it a reordering of the world, with everything exactly the same as in the former ordering. Those of them who were ashamed of the doctrine have said that a slight and very small difference arises from cycle to cycle compared with what was in the cycle before. These men say that in the next cycle things will be as follows: Socrates will again be the son of Sophroniscus and an Athenian, and Phaenarete, married to Sophroniscus, will give birth to him again.

So even if they do not use the name of resurrection, they point to the thing itself: Socrates, starting from the seed of Sophroniscus, will rise again and be formed in the womb of Phaenarete, and having been brought up in Athens he will be a philosopher, as though his former philosophy also were rising again and would be just the same as before. Anytus and Meletus too will rise again as accusers of Socrates, and the council of the Areopagus will condemn Socrates. What is more laughable still, Socrates will put on clothes exactly the same as in the former cycle, and he will live in exactly the same poverty and in exactly the same city of Athens as in the former cycle. Phalaris will be a tyrant again, and his bronze bull will bellow with the voices of those inside it, men exactly the same as those condemned in the former cycle. Alexander of Pherae will be a tyrant again, with cruelty exactly the same as before, condemning men exactly the same as those he condemned before.
Why need I list the Stoics’ philosophical teaching on such matters? Celsus does not laugh at it, but perhaps even reveres it, since Zeno seems to him wiser than Jesus.
translator_notes: The work on the resurrection Origen mentions is his lost treatise On the Resurrection. 'Those wise men' (τῶν σοφῶν ἐκείνων ἀνδρῶν) most likely means the wise writers of Scripture (such as Paul, just quoted), whose meaning simple believers do not represent; πρεσβεύεσθαι taken as 'represented' (also possible: 'upheld'). Origen's long protasis (Ἀλλ᾿ ἐπεὶ ... λέλεκται) with the staged text's full stop before τὰ δὲ τοῦ Κέλσου is rendered as separate sentences. ἀπαράλλακτος (repeated for rhetorical effect) rendered 'exactly the same' throughout. Historical note: Socrates was tried by a popular court, not the Areopagus; Origen's wording is kept. Phalaris was tyrant of Acragas; Alexander of Pherae a fourth-century BC tyrant in Thessaly. The Stoic doctrine of conflagration and identical recurrence is reported, not quoted; no classical source cited inline. Zeno = Zeno of Citium, founder of the Stoa; 'wiser than Jesus' is Origen's description of Celsus's view, not a quotation. Staged text has typo το for τὸ (δόγμα).

title: When the stars return to their places
english: The followers of Pythagoras and Plato too, though they seem to hold that the world is incorruptible, still fall into much the same notions. For they say that when the stars, in certain appointed cycles, take on the same configurations and positions toward one another, all things on earth are in the same state as they were when the world held that same arrangement of the stars. By this argument, then, when after a long cycle the stars come to the same position toward one another as they had in Socrates’ time, Socrates must be born again of the same parents and suffer the same things, accused by Anytus and Meletus and condemned by the council of the Areopagus.

The learned men of the Egyptians who hand down such teachings are held in honour and are not laughed at by Celsus and those like him. But we say that the universe is ordered by God in proportion to the state of what lies in each person’s power, and is always led, as far as is possible, toward what is better; and we know that the nature of what lies in our power admits of whatever it admits, for it cannot hold the utter changelessness of God. Yet we are not thought to say anything worth testing and examining.
translator_notes: τὸ ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν ('what lies in our power', the Greek term for free choice) rendered 'what lies in each person's power' / 'in our power' rather than the later system term 'free will'. ἐνδεχομένου ἃ ἐνδέχεται taken as: our power of choice is open to change as far as its nature allows, unlike God's changelessness. ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν rendered 'of the same parents' (the Greek says 'from the same'; parents implied by 5.20). The Pythagorean-Platonic 'great year' of star recurrence is reported, not quoted; no classical source cited inline (Plato, Timaeus 39d speaks of the perfect year, but Origen does not cite it). The staged text ends the chapter with a colon; the final clause (we are not thought worth examining) is kept as a statement. The long Greek sentence beginning ἡμεῖς δέ is split into two English sentences, with 'Yet' marking the contrast carried by the δέ clause.

title: Words that will not pass away
english: Let no one suspect, when we say this, that we belong to those who are called Christians but reject the doctrine of the resurrection taught in the Scriptures. For on their own premises they have no way at all to show how a stalk or a tree rises, as it were, from a grain “of wheat or of some other kind” (1 Corinthians 15:37).

But we are persuaded that what is sown “is not made alive unless it dies” (1 Corinthians 15:36), and that what is sown is “not the body that is to be” (1 Corinthians 15:37); for “God gives it a body as he willed” (1 Corinthians 15:38), raising it “in incorruption” after it has been sown “in corruption,” raising it “in glory” after it has been sown “in dishonour,” raising it “in power” after it has been sown “in weakness,” and raising it “spiritual” after it has been sown “a natural body” (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). So we keep both the mind of the church of Christ and the greatness of God’s promise, and we show that it is possible, not by bare assertion but by argument as well. For we know that even if “heaven and earth” pass away, and the things in them, still the “words,” the principles of each thing, which stand to the Word who was “in the beginning” “with God,” God the Word (John 1:1), as parts to a whole or species to a genus, will never pass away. For we choose to listen to him who said: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away” (Matthew 24:35; Mark 13:31; Luke 21:33).
translator_notes: Origen plays on λόγοι: the rational principles of each thing and Christ's 'words' (Matthew 24:35); the English keeps 'words' in quotation marks and adds 'the principles of each thing' as an appositive to carry both senses, since a single English word cannot. θεοῦ λόγου after 'with God' echoes John 1:1 ('and the Word was God'), rendered 'God the Word'. The staged text has a full stop before ὅσον ἐπὶ τῷ ἀρέσκοντι ἑαυτῶν, which belongs to the preceding clause ('on their own premises'); a stray opening quotation mark before καὶ ὅτι is ignored. οὐκ ἀποφάσει ἀλλὰ καὶ λόγῳ rendered 'not by bare assertion but by argument as well' (καί implies 'also'). 'Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away' matches Matthew 24:35 word for word; Mark 13:31 and Luke 21:33 are close parallels with small differences in wording; all three cited. The Christians who reject the resurrection are not named; Origen likely has in mind groups that denied any bodily resurrection.

title: The seed, the Stoics, and what God can do
english: We, then, do not say that the corrupted body returns “to its original nature,” any more than the corrupted grain of wheat returns to being a grain of wheat (1 Corinthians 15:37; John 12:24). For we say that, just as an ear rises from the grain of wheat, so a certain principle lies within the body; and from this principle, which is not corrupted, the body “is raised in incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15:42).

The Stoics, however, say that the body “wholly corrupted” returns “to its original nature,” because of the doctrines they hold about things that recur without variation in each cycle; and they say that “that very first make-up from which it was dissolved” will be put together again, establishing these things, as they suppose, by the necessities of logic.

Nor do we retreat to “a most absurd refuge” when we say that “everything is possible to God” (Matthew 19:26; Mark 10:27). For we know how to understand that “everything”: it does not refer to things that have no existence, nor to things that cannot be conceived. We say, too, that God cannot do shameful things, since then God would be able not to be God; for if God does anything shameful, he is not God.

But since Celsus lays it down that God does not will “what is against nature” either, we draw a distinction in what is said. If someone calls wickedness against nature, we too say that God does not will what is against nature, neither what springs from wickedness nor what happens without reason. But if one means what happens in accordance with God’s reason and his will, then such things must at once be not against nature; for what God does is not against nature, even if it is extraordinary, or seems extraordinary to some.

And if we must use a forced term, we will say that, compared with nature as it is more commonly understood, there are some things above nature which God might at some time do: raising man above human nature, causing him to change into a better and more divine nature, and keeping him so, as long as the one so kept also shows by his deeds that he wills it.
translator_notes: Origen answers Celsus's words quoted at 5.14; phrases lifted verbatim from that passage ('to its original nature', 'wholly corrupted', 'that very first make-up from which it was dissolved', 'a most absurd refuge', 'everything is possible to God', 'what is against nature') are set in double quotation marks as Celsus's words, though Koetschau does not mark them, and they follow the wording used for 5.14 in this translation. διαφθαρέν and φθειρομένου rendered with 'corrupted' so that the link to 'incorruption' (1 Corinthians 15:42) and to Celsus's 'wholly corrupted' stays visible. παρὰ φύσιν rendered 'against nature' throughout, matching 5.14. 'Grain of wheat' (κόκκος τοῦ σίτου) is set in quotation marks in the edition; it echoes both 1 Corinthians 15:37 (already quoted at 5.22) and John 12:24, so both are cited. 'Everything is possible to God' is the Christian saying Celsus mocks; the closest Gospel wording is Matthew 19:26 / Mark 10:27 (compare also Luke 1:37); cited as an allusion. λόγος τις in the body rendered 'a certain principle' (the seminal principle, as in 5.22); ἀφ᾿ οὗ kept as 'from this principle'. κατὰ λόγον θεοῦ rendered 'in accordance with God's reason', since it is set against ἀλόγως ('without reason'); not capitalised as the Word. παράδοξα rendered 'extraordinary'. βεβιασμένως ὀνομάσαι: 'use a forced term'. τῶν κατὰ περίοδον ἀπαραλλάκτων: the Stoic doctrine of identical recurrence in each world-cycle. 'God would be able not to be God' is a possible echo of 2 Timothy 2:13 ('he cannot deny himself'), not cited inline because the wording does not match. Koetschau 'τᾷ θεῷ' is a misprint for τῷ θεῷ in the staged text; no effect on sense. 'οὐ (γὰρ)': Koetschau's supplement, translated.

title: God wills nothing unworthy of himself
english: Having once said that God wills nothing that is unbefitting to himself, since such a thing would destroy his very being as God, we will say that if a man in his own depravity wills something vile, God will not be able to do it. So we are not bent on quarrelling with what Celsus says; rather, examining his words out of love for the truth, we will agree that God is not the God “of faulty appetite, nor of wandering disorder, but of right and just nature,” since he is the author of all that is good. And we confess another thing: that he can “grant everlasting life to a soul”; and not only can he, but he does grant it.

Because of what we have said already, nothing at all troubles us, not even the saying of Heraclitus which Celsus has taken over, that “corpses are more fit to be thrown out than dung” (Heraclitus, fragment 96). And yet one might say about this too that dung is indeed fit to be thrown out, but the corpses of human beings are not, because of the soul that dwelt in them, especially if that soul was a finer one. For under the more civilised of laws they are thought worthy of burial, with such honour as is possible for such things, so that we may not, in effect, insult the soul that dwelt within by casting away the body after the soul has left it, as we do the bodies of cattle.

Let it be granted, then, that God does not will “to make everlasting against reason” the grain of wheat, but rather the ear that comes from it; nor what is sown “in corruption,” but what is raised from it “in incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15:42). Further, the reason of all things is, according to Celsus, God himself; but according to us it is his Son, the Word, about whom we say in our philosophy: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). And according to us too, God “can do nothing contrary to reason, nor contrary to himself.”
translator_notes: Celsus's words from 5.14 that Origen repeats verbatim are set in quotation marks and follow the 5.14 rendering ('of faulty appetite, nor of wandering disorder, but of right and just nature', 'grant everlasting life to a soul', 'to make everlasting against reason', 'can do nothing contrary to reason, nor contrary to himself'). In Celsus the genitives depend on ἀρχηγέτης ('author of right and just nature'); Origen moves ἀρχηγέτης to 'every good', so the genitives stand alone; rendered 'the God of ...', with the quotation marks opening at 'of'. Origen has δύναται ('can') where Celsus had δύναιτ᾿ ἂν ('could'), so 'can' stands outside the quotation. The first sentence ('if a man in his own depravity wills something vile') paraphrases Celsus (βούληται for his ἐπιθυμήσῃς) and is left unquoted; βδελυρόν rendered 'vile' as at 5.14. Heraclitus fragment 96 (Diels–Kranz 22 B96); the citation is certain. ἀστειοτέρα (of the soul) and ἀστειοτέρους (of laws) are the same word; rendered 'finer' and 'more civilised' for English sense, losing the echo. τῇ δυνάμει taken as 'in effect, virtually'. μὴ βουλέσθω (third-person imperative) rendered as a concession, 'Let it be granted that God does not will'. ὁ τῶν πάντων λόγος: λόγος means both 'reason' (Celsus's sense) and 'Word' (John 1:1); 'the Word' added after 'his Son' only to carry the single Greek term into English, not as new content. πρὸς τὸν θεόν rendered 'with God'.

title: Celsus on the ancestral laws of the Jews
english: Let us look also at Celsus’s next passage, which runs as follows: “Now the Jews, having become a nation of their own and having laid down laws according to their local custom, still maintain them among themselves to this day; and in keeping a form of worship, whatever kind it may be, but at any rate ancestral, they act like the rest of mankind, since each people honours its ancestral customs, however they happen to have been established. And to do so seems to be of benefit too, not only because different people have come to think in different ways, and what has been publicly ratified must be preserved, but also because, as is likely, the parts of the earth were allotted from the beginning to different overseers and, being divided into certain dominions, are administered in this way. And indeed what is done among each people would be done rightly when it is done in the way that pleases them; and it is not holy to abolish the customs established in each place from the beginning.”

In these words Celsus implies that the Jews, who were Egyptians of old, later became a nation of their own, and that having laid down laws they maintain them. And, so as not to repeat Celsus’s words set out above, he says that it benefits them to practise their ancestral worship, like the other nations who honour their own customs. He also sets out a deeper cause why it benefits the Jews to honour their ancestral customs, hinting that those who were allotted to be overseers of the land of the peoples receiving laws laid down each people’s laws, working together with the lawgivers. He seems, then, to show that the land of the Jews too, and the nation living in it, is overseen by someone, or by several, and that the laws of the Jews were laid down by that one or those several, working together with Moses.
