translator_notes: Quotation from Celsus set in double quotation marks. καθεστηκότα is Koetschau's supplement, translated as 'however they happen to have been established'. τὰ ἐς κοινὸν κεκυρωμένα rendered 'what has been publicly ratified' (not 'for the common good', which adds a notion). ὅπῃ ἐκείνοις φίλον: 'them' is ambiguous in Celsus (the peoples or the overseers); left ambiguous here, since Origen reads it of the overseers at 5.27. οὐχ ὅσιον rendered 'not holy' throughout 5.25-28 to keep the ὅσιον/ἀνόσιον (holy/unholy) contrast Origen builds on; εὐσέβεια is kept as 'piety'. ἐπόπται rendered 'overseers'. The claim that the Jews were Egyptians refers back to Celsus at 3.5. τῶν νομοθετουμένων stands directly after τῆς γῆς and is taken with it ('the land of the peoples receiving laws'); it could instead go with τοῖς νομοθέταις ('the lawgivers of those receiving laws'), with no real change of sense. No Scripture quoted.

title: Who divided the earth among its overseers?
english: “And the laws must be kept,” he says, “not only because different people have come to think in different ways, and because what has been publicly ratified must be preserved, but also because, as is likely, the parts of the earth were allotted from the beginning to different overseers and, being divided into certain dominions, are administered in this way.” Then, as though he had forgotten what he said against the Jews, Celsus now includes them too in his general praise of all who keep their ancestral customs, saying: “And indeed what is done among each people would be done rightly when it is done in the way that pleases them.”

And see whether he does not plainly wish, as far as it rests with him, that the Jew who lives under his own laws should not depart from them, since he would be doing what is not holy if he departed. For he says that “it is not holy to abolish the customs established in each place from the beginning.”

On this I should like to ask him, or those who think as he does: who, then, was it who from the beginning distributed the parts of the earth to different overseers, and clearly also gave the land of the Jews, and the Jews themselves, to the one or the several who received it by lot? Was it, to use the name Celsus would give him, Zeus who gave the nation of the Jews and their land to someone, or to several, and did he will that the one who received Judaea should lay down such laws among the Jews? Or did this come about against his will? Whichever way he answers, you see that his argument will be hard pressed.

But if the parts of the earth were not distributed to their overseers by some one being, then each of them took a share of the earth haphazardly, as it happened, with no one presiding. Yet this too is absurd, and goes some way toward doing away with the providence of the God who is over all.
translator_notes: Celsus's words (repeated from 5.25) set in double quotation marks; 'And the laws must be kept' is Origen's lead-in to the repeated words, introduced by φησί, and is kept inside the quotation as Origen frames it. 'What he said against the Jews': Celsus's attacks on the Jews in earlier books. ἀποκληρωτικῶς: 'arbitrarily, at random' (as by casting lots), rendered 'haphazardly'; ὡς ἔτυχε 'as it happened'; διενείματο (middle) taken as 'took a share for himself'. μετρίως ... ἀναιρετικόν: literally 'moderately destructive'; rendered 'goes some way toward doing away with', which keeps Origen's measured word rather than strengthening it. ὁ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεός rendered 'the God who is over all' (capitalised: the true God). Ζεύς kept as 'Zeus', Celsus's name for the supreme god. No Scripture quoted.

title: If every ancestral law were holy
english: How, and under what dominions, the parts of the earth are divided and administered by those who oversee them, let anyone who wishes explain. And let him tell us also how what is done among each people is done rightly when done in the way that pleases the overseers, and whether, for example, the laws of the Scythians about killing their fathers are right, or those of the Persians, which do not forbid mothers to be married by their own sons, or daughters by their own fathers.

And why need I gather instances from those who have written treatises on the laws of the various nations, and press the difficulty further: how are the laws among each people rightly kept, in the way that pleases the overseers? Let Celsus tell us how it is not holy to abolish ancestral laws about marrying mothers and daughters, or about its being blessed to depart this life by hanging, or about the claim that those who give themselves up to the fire and to release from life through fire are wholly purified. And how is it not holy to abolish laws such as those among the Taurians about offering strangers as sacrifices to Artemis, or among some of the Libyans about sacrificing children to Cronus?

Yet it does follow from Celsus’s view that it is not holy for the Jews to abolish their ancestral laws, which say that one must worship no other god besides the Maker of the universe. And on his account what is holy will be divine not by nature but by some enactment and custom. For among some it is holy to revere the crocodile and to eat something that others worship; among others it is holy to revere the calf; and among others again, to consider the goat a god. And so the same man will be doing holy things with regard to these laws, and unholy things with regard to others; which is the most absurd thing of all.
translator_notes: Echoes of Celsus's phrases ('under certain dominions', 'in the way that pleases', 'it is not holy to abolish') are given in Origen's syntax and not set as fresh quotations, since Origen is now turning them into questions. Scythian parricide and Persian next-of-kin marriage are common ethnographic topics; Origen names no source and none is cited. The Taurian sacrifice of strangers to Artemis is the story of Euripides' Iphigenia among the Taurians and Herodotus 4.103, but Origen cites neither, so no inline source is given. The hanging and fire customs are left unidentified (fire may refer to Indian ascetics). περὶ τοῦ ... πάντως καθαίρεσθαι (article with infinitive) rendered 'about the claim that ... are wholly purified', parallel to 'about its being blessed'. οἰκείοις is Koetschau's supplement, translated as 'their own'. οὐ φύσει τὸ ὅσιον ἀλλά τινι θέσει καὶ νομίσει θεῖον is awkward in Greek (θεῖον may be corrupt or predicative); rendered 'what is holy will be divine not by nature but by some enactment and custom'. σέβειν rendered 'revere' and προσκυνουμένων 'worship', to keep the two verbs apart; τι (the thing eaten) left as 'something', not narrowed to 'creatures'. θεός lower-case in 'no other god' and 'consider the goat a god' (generic and pagan); δημιουργός rendered 'Maker'. (ὁ) is Koetschau's supplement. The Egyptian crocodile and calf cults and the goat of Mendes stand behind the examples. Kronos rendered 'Cronus'. No Scripture quoted.

title: Holiness is not a matter of custom
english: But they will probably say in reply that the man who keeps his ancestral customs is holy, and not unholy in any way for failing to keep the customs of others as well; and again, that the man considered unholy by certain people is not unholy when, following his ancestral customs, he worships what is his own, and makes war on and feasts upon what is revered among those whose laws are the opposite of his.

But see whether this does not reveal great confusion about what is just and holy, and about piety, as though piety had no clear definition, nor any nature of its own that marks out as pious those who act in accordance with it. If, then, piety and holiness and justice belong among relative things, so that the same thing is holy and unholy according to different relations and laws, see whether temperance too will not consequently be relative, and courage, and prudence, and knowledge, and the rest of the virtues; and nothing could be more absurd than that.

Now, for those who take a simpler and more ordinary stand against the words of Celsus set out above, what has been said is enough. But since we think that some readers of a more searching kind will also come upon this writing, let us venture to set out a few of the deeper matters, which hold a certain mystical and secret insight, about the regions of the earth having been allotted from the beginning to different overseers; and let us, as far as we are able, present the teaching clear of the absurdities we have listed.
translator_notes: ἐπεὶ μὴ (καὶ) τὰ ἑτέρων οὐ τηρεῖ: καί is Koetschau's supplement and the double negative is awkward; read as 'he is not unholy on the ground that he does not also keep the customs of others', rendered 'not unholy in any way for failing to keep the customs of others as well' so the English cannot be read as giving the reason he is not unholy. τὰ ... προσπολεμῇ καὶ καταθοινᾶται: 'makes war on and feasts upon' what others revere (e.g. eating animals that another people worships, as in 5.27); 'revered' is supplied from the contrast with τὰ μὲν ἴδια σέβῃ. τῶν πρός τι: the Aristotelian category of relatives, rendered 'relative things'. Temperance, courage and prudence, with justice already named beside piety, are the classical cardinal virtues; knowledge (ἐπιστήμη) is added to them. μυστικὴν καὶ ἀπόῤῥητον θεωρίαν rendered 'a certain mystical and secret insight' (θεωρία: contemplative insight into a deeper meaning). μὲν οὖν opening the third paragraph rendered 'Now', not 'For'. This chapter introduces Origen's reading of Deuteronomy 32:8-9 and Genesis 11 in 5.29; no Scripture is quoted here.

title: Moses on the dividing of the nations
english: Celsus seems to me to have misheard certain more mystical teachings about how the things on earth were apportioned. Greek history too touches on these in some way, when it brings in some of those reputed to be gods contending with one another over Attica, and when in the poets it makes some of the so-called gods admit that certain places are more their own. Barbarian history also, and above all that of the Egyptians, shows something of the kind about the division of what are called the nomes of Egypt, saying that Athena, who obtained Sais by lot, is the same who also holds Attica. The learned men of the Egyptians will tell countless things of this sort, though I do not know whether they also include the Jews and their land when they assign lands to one being or another. But enough for the present about what is said on these matters outside the divine word.

We say that Moses, the prophet of God among us and his true servant, sets out in the song of Deuteronomy the following about the division of the earth: “When the Most High divided the nations, when he scattered the sons of Adam, he set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God; and his people Jacob became the Lord’s portion, Israel the measured lot of his inheritance” (Deuteronomy 32:8–9).

And the same Moses, in the book entitled Genesis, tells of the division of the nations in the form of a history, as follows: “And all the earth had one language, and there was one speech for all. And it came to pass, as they moved from the east, that they found a plain in the land of Shinar, and they settled there” (Genesis 11:1–2). And a little after: “The Lord came down,” it says, “to see the city and the tower which the sons of men had built. And the Lord said: Behold, they are one race and all have one language; and this they have begun to do, and now nothing that they set out to do will fail them. Come, let us go down and confound their tongue there, so that none of them may understand the speech of his neighbour. And the Lord scattered them from there over the face of all the earth, and they stopped building the city and the tower. For this reason its name was called Confusion, because there the Lord God confounded the language of all the earth, and from there the Lord God scattered them over the face of all the earth” (Genesis 11:5–9).

And in the book entitled the Wisdom of Solomon, where it speaks of wisdom and of the events at the confusion of tongues, when the division of those on earth took place, this is said about wisdom: “She also, when the nations had been confounded in their agreement in wickedness, knew the righteous man, and kept him blameless before God, and kept him strong against his tender love for his child” (Wisdom of Solomon 10:5).

The teaching on these matters is long and mystical, and to it applies the saying, “It is good to keep hidden the secret of a king” (Tobit 12:7). This is so that the teaching about souls that are bound into a body, not by transmigration, may not be thrown to whatever ears happen to hear it, and what is holy may not be given “to the dogs,” nor pearls thrown before swine (Matthew 7:6). For such a thing is impious, since it means betraying the secret oracles of the wisdom of God, of which it is well written: “Wisdom will not enter a soul that plots evil, nor dwell in a body in debt to sin” (Wisdom of Solomon 1:4). It is enough to present in the manner of a history what is told in a hidden way as though it were history, so that those who are able may work out for themselves what bears on the passage.
translator_notes: Deuteronomy 32:8 follows the LXX 'according to the number of the angels of God' (Hebrew/MT: 'sons of Israel'); kept as Origen reads it, since his argument rests on it. σχοίνισμα ('portion measured by line') rendered 'measured lot', kept the same in 5.31. Genesis 11 is quoted from the LXX: χεῖλος (literally 'lip') rendered 'language', φωνή 'speech'; ἀπ᾿ ἀνατολῶν kept as 'from the east' because Origen's allegory in 5.30-31 depends on it; Σύγχυσις ('Confusion') is the LXX's rendering of the name Babel; Origen skips Genesis 11:3-4 here ('a little after') and uses them in 5.30. The Wisdom of Solomon sentence has a doubled γῆς in the staged text (ὁ μερισμὸς τῶν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, γῆς.), taken as dittography and translated once. Wisdom 10:5 refers to Abraham and Isaac; Origen's text reads ἐφύλαξεν where printed LXX has ἐτήρησεν in the first clause; sense unchanged. 'It is good to keep hidden the secret of a king' is Tobit 12:7 (also 12:11). 'Holy things to the dogs ... pearls before swine' is Matthew 7:6, given in Origen's own wording (παραβάλλωνται χοίροις). 'Our prophet of God and his true servant Moses' may echo Numbers 12:7 and Hebrews 3:5 (θεράπων); possible allusion only, not cited inline. Classical background left uncited because not certain from the Greek alone: the contest of Athena and Poseidon over Attica (told e.g. in Herodotus 8.55 and Apollodorus), gods in the poets naming favourite places (perhaps Hera's cities in Iliad 4.51-52), and the Greek identification of the goddess of Sais with Athena (compare Plato, Timaeus 21e). 'The teaching about souls bound into a body, though not by transmigration': ψυχῶν οὐκ ἐκ μετενσωματώσεως εἰς σῶμα ἐνδουμένων, translated literally; Origen distinguishes his view from transmigration. τινῶν in the first sentence taken with μυστικωτέρων λόγων ('certain teachings'), not as 'from certain people'.

title: Leaving the east and building the tower
english: Let us think of all those on earth, then, as using one divine language; and for as long as they are in harmony with one another, let them be kept in that divine language. And let them remain unmoved from “the east” so long as their minds are set on the things of the light, and of the radiance that comes from “eternal light” (Wisdom of Solomon 7:26). And when these move themselves “from the east,” setting their minds on things foreign to “the east,” let them find “a plain in the land of Shinar” (Genesis 11:2), a name which means “shaking out of teeth,” as a symbol that they lose the things by which they are fed; and let them settle there.

Then, wishing to gather together the things of matter, and to fasten to heaven what by nature cannot be fastened to it, so that by material things they may plot against things that are immaterial, let them say: “Come, let us make bricks and bake them with fire” (Genesis 11:3). So then, as they harden and make solid what is of clay and of matter, and want to make the brick into stone and the clay into bitumen (Genesis 11:3), and by these means to build “a city and a tower whose top,” as far as their own notion goes, “shall reach to heaven” (Genesis 11:4), in the manner of the heights that are lifted up “against the knowledge of God” (2 Corinthians 10:5), let them be handed over, each of them, to angels: angels harsher in a greater or lesser degree, and of one kind or another, in proportion to the movement “from the east” that has taken place in them to a greater or lesser degree, and in proportion to their making bricks into stones and clay into bitumen, and to their building from these, until they pay the penalty for what they have dared.

And let them be led, each of them, by the angels who implanted in them their own language, to the parts of the earth according to what each deserves: some, let us say, to a scorching land, others to a land that punishes those who live in it by its cold; some to a land harder to farm, others to one less so; some to a land full of wild beasts, others to one with fewer of them.
translator_notes: The chapter is an allegory of Genesis 11:1-9 told in third-person imperatives ('let them be thought of ... let them find ... let them be handed over'); kept as 'let ...' to preserve Origen's hypothetical, teaching form. 'Radiance of eternal light' (ἀπαύγασμα φωτὸς ἀϊδίου) is Wisdom of Solomon 7:26 (compare Hebrews 1:3, ἀπαύγασμα; not cited inline). Genesis 11:2-4 quoted from the LXX; Genesis 11:3 LXX has 'the brick became stone for them, and bitumen was their mortar (πηλός)'; Origen turns it into 'make brick into stone and clay into bitumen'. 'Shaking out of teeth' (ὀδόντων ἐκτιναγμός) is Origen's etymology of Shinar (Sennaar), from an onomastic tradition; given as he states it. 'Heights lifted up against the knowledge of God' adapts 2 Corinthians 10:5 (πᾶν ὕψωμα ἐπαιρόμενον κατὰ τῆς γνώσεως τοῦ θεοῦ); Origen writes ὑπεραιρόμενα ὑψώματα. The staged text shows a stray full stop before ἐς ὅσον and a spaced comma after θεοῦ; read as one sentence each. τῶν ἐμποιησάντων τὴν οἰκείαν ἑαυτοῖς διάλεκτον taken as 'the angels who implanted in them their own language' (i.e. each group's angels gave it its tongue; ἑαυτοῖς most naturally means the angels' own language, and the English 'their own' keeps that open).

title: The Lord’s portion and its exile
english: Next, if anyone can, as under the figure of a history which has something true in itself and yet also points to something secret, let him see also those who kept the original language: because they did not move “from the east,” they remained in the east and in the eastern language. And let him understand that these alone became the Lord’s portion and his people called “Jacob,” and became also “Israel, the measured lot of his inheritance” (Deuteronomy 32:9). And let these alone be governed by a ruler who did not receive those under him for punishment, as the others did.

Let him who is able see also the sins, such as happen among human beings, committed in the commonwealth of those assigned to the portion that belongs to the Lord. At first they were tolerable, and of such a kind that the people did not altogether deserve to be forsaken; later they were more numerous, but still tolerable. And understanding that this went on for a long time, and that healing was always being applied, and that at intervals they turned back, let him see them abandoned, in proportion to their sins, to those who had received the other lands by lot: at first punished lightly and paying the penalty, and then, as if they had been disciplined, returning to their own land. But later let him see them handed over to harsher rulers, whom the Scriptures would name Assyrians and then Babylonians.

Then, though remedies were applied, let him see them increasing their sins none the less, and for this reason scattered among the other portions by the rulers of the other nations who plundered them. And let their own ruler deliberately overlook their being plundered by the rulers in the other nations, so that he too, with good reason and as if avenging himself, may receive authority to draw away from the other nations all whom he can, and may do so, and give them laws and show them the life they must live, in order to lead them up to the goal to which he used to lead those of the former nation who did not sin.
translator_notes: Deuteronomy 32:9 (LXX) is taken up again from 5.29; 'measured lot' kept for σχοίνισμα. Origen continues the third-person imperatives ('let him see ... let their ruler overlook'), kept as such. The cycle of sin, light punishment and return probably reflects the pattern of Judges, and the exiles to Assyria and Babylon (2 Kings 17 and 25), but these are narrative summaries, not quotations, so no verse is cited inline. ἐπισπειρομένους ('sown in among', 'scattered among') rendered 'scattered among'; the construction ὑπὸ τῶν διαρπαζόντων αὐτοὺς ἀρχόντων τῶν λοιπῶν ἐθνῶν ταῖς ἄλλαις μερίσιν read as agent (rulers of the other nations) plus destination (the other portions). ὡς ἐν ἀνθρώποις taken as 'such as happen among human beings'. ἐπὶ πλείονα χρόνον rendered 'for a long time' (comparative used loosely). 'Ruler' (ἄρχων) of the Lord's portion is left lowercase, since Origen speaks in figure and does not name him here; in 5.32 he identifies the one more powerful than all rulers with Jesus.

title: Christ frees the nations from their overseers
english: And from this let those who are able to see things so great learn that he who received by lot those who had not sinned before is far more powerful than the rest. For he has been able to take chosen ones from everyone’s portion, to withdraw them from those who had received them for punishment, and to bring them to laws and to a life that helps toward an amnesty for the sins they had committed before. But, as we said earlier, let these things be spoken by us in a veiled way.

These things make clear what was misheard by those who said that “the parts of the earth were from the beginning allotted to different overseers, divided into certain dominions, and administered in this way”; from them Celsus too took the words already set out. But since those who moved “from the east” were handed over, because of their sins, “to a debased mind” (Romans 1:28), and “to dishonourable passions” (Romans 1:26), and “in the lusts of their hearts to impurity” (Romans 1:24), so that, having had their fill of sin, they might hate it, we will not submit to Celsus’s opinion when he says that because of the overseers allotted to the parts of the earth, what is done among each people is done rightly. On the contrary, we positively wish not to do what comes from those overseers “in the way that pleases them.”

For we see that it is holy to abolish “the customs established in each place from the beginning” by better and more divine laws, which Jesus laid down as one most powerful, when he rescued “us from the present evil age” (Galatians 1:4) and from “the rulers of this age, who are being brought to nothing” (1 Corinthians 2:6); and that it is unholy not to cast oneself upon him who has appeared and been shown to be purer and more powerful than all rulers. To him God said, as the prophets foretold many generations before: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Psalm 2:8). For “he himself” has become the “expectation” (Genesis 49:10) of us who from “the nations” have believed in him and in God over all, his Father.
translator_notes: The words in quotation marks in the second paragraph reproduce Celsus's own phrasing from 5.25 (τὰ μέρη τῆς γῆς ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἄλλα ἄλλοις ἐπόπταις νενεμημένα καὶ κατά τινας ἐπικρατείας διειλημμένα ταύτῃ καὶ διοικεῖται; ὅπῃ ἐκείνοις φίλον; τὰ ἐξ ἀρχῆς κατὰ τόπους νενομισμένα). Origen reverses Celsus's 'it is not holy to abolish' (παραλύειν δὲ οὐχ ὅσιον) into 'it is holy to abolish' (λύειν); the quoted phrases are worded as in the 5.25 translation so readers can see the echo. The clause 'that what is done among each people is done rightly' paraphrases Celsus (ὀρθῶς ἂν πράττοιτο), so it is left unquoted. ἐκείνοις / (παρ᾿) ἐκείνων taken to mean the overseers, as in Celsus's sentence; (παρ᾿) is an editorial supplement. (λαβὼν) and (καθαρωτέρῳ καὶ) are editorial supplements in the staged text, both translated. Romans 1:24, 26, 28 quoted in reverse order, as Origen gives them. 'From the present evil age' is Galatians 1:4 (ἐκ τοῦ αἰῶνος τοῦ ἐνεστῶτος πονηροῦ; Origen ἀπό). 'The rulers of this age who are being brought to nothing' is 1 Corinthians 2:6. Psalm 2:8: LXX and English numbering agree. 'He himself ... the expectation of the nations' is Genesis 49:10 LXX (αὐτὸς προσδοκία ἐθνῶν), which differs from the Hebrew; Origen splits the phrase across the sentence. 'God over all' (ὁ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεός) may echo Romans 9:5 or Ephesians 4:6; not cited inline. ἀμνηστία rendered 'amnesty' (a pardon that blots out the record), its exact sense.

title: Where the Christians come from
english: What we have said was said not only in answer to what was set out about the overseers; it also in some measure anticipates what Celsus says against us. For he says: “Let the second party come forward. I will ask them where they have come from, or whom they have as the founder of their ancestral laws. They will name no one, since they themselves set out from there and bring their teacher and chorus leader from nowhere else; and yet they have broken away from the Jews.”

We, then, have come, each of us, “in the last days,” when our Jesus has come to visit us, to “the manifest mountain of the Lord” (Isaiah 2:2), that is, to the Word who is “above” every word, and to the house “of God,” which “is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth” (1 Timothy 3:15). And we see in what way this house is built “on the tops of the mountains,” that is, on all the prophetic words, which are its foundation. And this “house” is raised “above the hills” (Isaiah 2:2), that is, above those who appear to profess something exceptional among men in wisdom and truth.

And we, “all the nations,” come to it, and we, the many nations, go, and say to one another, as we urge each other on toward the worship of God that shone out “in the last days” through Jesus Christ: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will declare his way to us, and we will walk in it” (Isaiah 2:2–3). For the “law” went out from those in “Zion” and passed over to us as a spiritual law (Isaiah 2:3). And “the word of the Lord” also went out from that “Jerusalem” (Isaiah 2:3), so that it might spread everywhere and judge “between the nations,” choosing those whom he sees are ready to obey, and reproving the “many people” who will not obey (Isaiah 2:4).

And to those who ask us where we have come from, or whom we have as our founder, we say that we have come, following the counsels of Jesus, to beat our warlike and insolent “swords” of speech “into ploughshares,” and we are refashioning “the spears” of our former fighting “into sickles” (Isaiah 2:4). For we no longer take up “sword against nation,” nor do we learn “to make war any more” (Isaiah 2:4), since because of Jesus we have become sons of peace. He is our founder; and in place of the ancestral laws, under which we were “strangers to the covenants” (Ephesians 2:12), we have received a law, for which we give thanks to him who rescued us from error, and say: “How false were the idols our fathers acquired, and there is none among them that sends rain” (Jeremiah 16:19; 14:22).

So our chorus leader and teacher, having gone out from the Jews, holds the whole inhabited world as his own by the word of his teaching. In saying this in advance, we have overturned, as far as we could, a passage of Celsus that comes much later, joining it to his statements already set out.
translator_notes: Celsus's words (ἴτω δὲ ὁ δεύτερος ... ἀφεστήκασιν Ἰουδαίων) are quoted from a later place in his book, as Origen says at the end of the chapter; set in quotation marks. 'The second party' (ὁ δεύτερος): Celsus has dealt with the Jews and now calls on the Christians; the masculine may imply 'second chorus', matching χοροστάτης, but the noun is not expressed. ἀρχηγέτης (Celsus) and ἀρχηγός (Origen, of Jesus) both rendered 'founder' to keep Origen's answer to Celsus's question visible; ἀρχηγός can also mean 'author' or 'leader' (compare Acts 3:15; Hebrews 2:10; 12:2; not cited). The chapter is built on Isaiah 2:2-4 LXX (parallel Micah 4:1-3), quoted in pieces and glossed: 'manifest mountain', 'on the tops of the mountains', 'above the hills', 'all the nations', 'many nations', 'Come, let us go up ...', 'law from Zion, word of the Lord from Jerusalem', 'judge between the nations, reprove many people', swords into ploughshares and spears (ζιβύνη) into sickles, no more sword against nation or learning war. Origen's interpretive glosses (the Word above every word; the prophetic words as foundation; the hills as those claiming wisdom; the law passing to us as spiritual) are kept as his. 1 Timothy 3:15 quoted exactly. 'Strangers to the covenants' is Ephesians 2:12. The closing prayer joins Jeremiah 16:19 LXX ('how false were the idols our fathers acquired', where the LXX ends 'and there is no profit in them') with Jeremiah 14:22 LXX ('is there among the idols of the nations one that sends rain?'). λογικὰς μαχαίρας ('rational/verbal swords') is doubtful: rendered 'swords of speech', meaning the hostile words of the former pagan life; Origen may mean that Christians once fought with words. Possible allusions not cited inline: 'children of peace' (Luke 10:6, 'son of peace'); 'the law ... spiritual' (Romans 7:14); 'prophetic words, which are its foundation' (Ephesians 2:20). νέμεται / νεμηθῇ continue the allotment theme of 5.25-32 (the Word now holds the whole world as his portion); rendered 'holds ... as his own' and 'spread'. The staged text punctuates 'θεοῦ. ὅς' and ἡμῶν, ἑαυτοῦ oddly; read as continuous sentences. ἀντὶ τῶν πατρίων is taken with λαμβάνοντες νόμον ('in place of the ancestral laws ... we have received a law'), answering Celsus's question about the founder of 'ancestral laws' (πατρίων νόμων). γενόμενοι διὰ τὸν Ἰησοῦν (accusative) rendered 'because of Jesus', not 'through'.

title: Celsus calls Herodotus to witness for ancestral custom
english: So that we do not pass over what Celsus said in the passage between, let us set this out as well. “One might also call on Herodotus as a witness to this, who says as follows: ‘The people of the city of Marea and of Apis, who live in the parts of Egypt bordering on Libya, thought themselves Libyans and not Egyptians, and chafed at the observance of the sacred rites, since they did not wish to be barred from cows. So they sent to Ammon, saying that they had nothing in common with the Egyptians, for they lived outside the Delta and did not agree with them, and that they wished to be allowed to taste of everything. But the god would not let them do this. He said that Egypt was the land which the Nile overflows and waters, and that those were Egyptians who live below the city of Elephantine and drink from this river’ (Herodotus, Histories 2.18). That is Herodotus’s account. But Ammon is no worse an envoy of divine things than the angels of the Jews, so that there is nothing wrong in each people practising its own customs.

“Indeed we shall find the greatest difference among them from nation to nation, and yet each people seems to think its own customs the best of all. Of the Ethiopians, those who live at Meroe worship ‘Zeus and Dionysus alone’ (Herodotus, Histories 2.29); the Arabians worship Urania and Dionysus, these alone (Herodotus, Histories 3.8). All the Egyptians worship Osiris and Isis; the people of Sais worship Athena; the people of Naucratis, who began not long ago, have named Serapis; and the rest each in their own way, nome by nome. Some abstain from sheep, revering them as sacred, others from goats, others from crocodiles, others from cows, and they abstain from pigs because they loathe them. Among the Scythians it is a fine thing even to feast on men, and there are Indians who think they do a holy thing by eating even their fathers.

“And somewhere the same Herodotus says (I will again use his very words, so as to be believed), and his account runs thus: ‘If one were to set before all men the task of choosing the finest customs out of all customs, each, after looking them over, would choose their own, so firmly does each people believe its own customs to be by far the finest. It is not likely, then, that anyone but a madman would make a mockery of such things. That all men hold this view about customs may be judged from many other proofs, and among them from this one. Darius, during his reign, called the Greeks who were present and asked them for what sum they would be willing to eat their fathers when they died. They said that they would not do it for any sum. After this Darius called the Indians known as Callatiae, who eat their parents, and asked them, while the Greeks were present and learned through an interpreter what was said, for what sum they would agree to burn their fathers with fire when they died. They cried out loudly and told him to speak no words of ill omen. So these things are fixed by custom, and Pindar, I think, put it rightly in his verse when he said that custom is king of all’ (Herodotus, Histories 3.38; Pindar, fragment 169).”
translator_notes: The whole chapter after Origen's first sentence is Celsus's text, with two long verbatim quotations of Herodotus nested inside it (single quotation marks). Celsus himself says he quotes Herodotus's very words (Herodotus, Histories 2.18 and 3.38); the intervening catalogue of cults draws on Herodotus 2.29 (Meroe: Zeus and Dionysus), 3.8 (Arabians: Dionysus and Urania), and Egyptian material in book 2, but the Serapis line is Celsus's own (Herodotus does not mention Serapis). Only the certain Herodotus loci are cited inline. Pindar's line 'custom is king of all' is Pindar, fragment 169 (Snell-Maehler 169a), quoted by Herodotus. Koetschau's text of Herodotus 3.38 carries editorial supplements in parentheses from the Herodotus manuscripts: (τῶν), (ἕκαστοι τοὺς ἑωυτῶν· οὕτω νομίζουσι), (τοὺς), (γέλωτα), (τῷδε); the translation follows the supplemented text, since without them the sentence does not construe. κόσῳ is Ionic for πόσῳ. θηλέων βοῶν μὴ ἔργεσθαι: 'not to be barred from cows', i.e. from eating them; the Egyptians did not eat cows (sacred to Isis). τὰ δαιμόνια in Celsus's mouth is neutral ('divine things'), rendered 'divine things', not 'demons'. εὐφημέειν literally 'to keep holy silence / speak well-omened words', rendered 'speak no words of ill omen'. ὠνόμασαν Σάραπιν rendered literally 'have named Serapis' (i.e. adopted him as their god). Typos in the staged Greek (κατα, ευ, ουν, καταλι πόντας in the next chapter) are spacing/accent losses from the TEI and do not affect sense. No Scripture in this chapter.

title: Philosophers do not keep foolish ancestral customs
english: By these words Celsus’s argument seems to be making its way to the claim that all men ought to live according to their ancestral customs, and would not be blamed for doing so, while the Christians, who have abandoned their ancestral customs and are not one particular nation, as the Jews are, are open to blame for attaching themselves to the teaching of Jesus.

Let him tell us, then: will those who study philosophy and are taught not to be superstitious be right to abandon their ancestral customs, so far as even to eat things forbidden in their homelands, or will they be doing what is not fitting? For if, because of philosophy and the lessons they learn against superstition, they do not keep their ancestral customs and would even eat what their fathers forbade them, why should Christians not do this without blame as well? For reason requires them not to busy themselves with statues and shrines, nor even with the works of God, but to rise above these and to present the soul to the Creator; in this they do what corresponds to what the philosophers do.

But suppose that Celsus, or those who approve of his views, will say, to protect the position he has set himself, that even a man who has taken up philosophy will keep his ancestral customs. Then it is high time for philosophers, among the Egyptians for instance, to become utterly ridiculous, taking care not to eat an onion, so as to keep their ancestral customs, or certain parts of the body, such as the head and the shoulder, so as not to break what their fathers handed down to them. And I am not yet speaking of those Egyptians who shudder at the trivial noises the body makes in passing wind, to point out that if one of these becomes a philosopher and keeps his ancestral customs, he would be a ridiculous philosopher doing unphilosophical things.

In the same way, then, a man who has been led by reason to worship the God of the universe, and who because of his ancestral customs stays somewhere down below among the statues and the shrines men have set up, and is unwilling to rise to the Creator by his own choice, would be like those who have learned the lessons of philosophy, yet fear what is not to be feared and think it impiety to eat this or that.
translator_notes: The first paragraph is Origen's summary of where Celsus's argument tends, not a quotation, so no quotation marks. λόγου αἱροῦντος (paragraph 2) and ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου προσαχθείς (paragraph 4) are rendered 'reason'; Origen may intend a play on the divine Word as well, but the parallel with the philosophers points first to reason, so lower-case 'reason' is kept in both places. τευτάζειν: 'to be busy/fuss about'. ἱδρύματα: things set up, i.e. shrines and erected images. φέρ᾿ εἰπεῖν taken as the idiom 'for instance', qualifying ἐν Αἰγυπτίοις (reviewer: the earlier 'it is time to say ... so to speak' rendered εἰπεῖν twice). The onion, head and shoulder: Egyptian food taboos; ἐμφαγεῖν governs both κρομύου and μορίων. τῶν τὰς τοῦ σώματος φλυαρίας ἐν φύσαις φριττόντων: those who shudder at the body's trifling noises in breaking wind (an Egyptian cult reported by later Christian writers); the translation keeps the sense without crudeness. Possible faint echo in 'present the soul to the Creator' of Romans 12:1 (παραστῆσαι τὰ σώματα), not cited inline as the wording differs. No Scripture cited.

title: Herodotus’s Ammon and the customs of Scythians and Indians
english: And what, too, is Herodotus’s Ammon like, whose words Celsus has taken over as if to prove that each people must keep its ancestral customs? For their Ammon does not allow the people from the city of Marea and from Apis, who live in the parts bordering on Libya, to treat the use of cows as indifferent; and yet this is a thing that is not only indifferent by its own nature, but also does not prevent anyone from being noble and good. If their Ammon had forbidden the use of cows because the animal is useful for farming, and besides because the stock increases mostly through the females, his word might perhaps have had some plausibility. But as it is, he simply insists that because they drink of the Nile they must keep the Egyptians’ laws about cows.

And it was on this point that Celsus, mocking the angels among the Jews who serve as envoys of the things of God, said that Ammon was no worse an envoy of divine things than the angels of the Jews. Yet he did not examine their words and their appearances, to see what they mean. For he would have seen that “God does not care for oxen” (1 Corinthians 9:9), even where He seems to be making laws about oxen or animals without reason (Deuteronomy 25:4), but that what was written for the sake of human beings (1 Corinthians 9:10), under the outward appearance of dealing with animals without reason, contains a teaching about the nature of things.

Celsus, then, says that each people does nothing wrong in wishing to practise its own customs. On his view it follows that the Scythians do nothing wrong, since they feast on men according to their ancestral customs. And those Indians who eat their fathers think they do a holy thing, and according to Celsus they do so, or at least do nothing wrong. At any rate he sets out a passage of Herodotus that argues that each people does right to follow its ancestral laws, and he seems to approve of the Indians of Darius’s time called Callatiae, who eat their parents, since, when Darius asked them for what sum they would be willing to give up this law, they cried out loudly and told him to speak no words of ill omen.
translator_notes: οὐ τῶν βοῶν μέλει τῷ θεῷ is Paul's question in 1 Corinthians 9:9 (μὴ τῶν βοῶν μέλει τῷ θεῷ;) turned into a statement; 'the law about oxen' it comments on is Deuteronomy 25:4 ('You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain'), cited at the clause 'making laws about oxen'. δι᾿ ἀνθρώπους γραφέντα echoes 1 Corinthians 9:10 (δι᾿ ἡμᾶς γὰρ ἐγράφη). φυσιολογίαν τινά: literally 'a certain natural philosophy / account of nature'; Origen means a deeper meaning about the nature of things (human and spiritual), rendered 'a teaching about the nature of things'. ὁ λόγος in 'his word might have had plausibility' could mean 'the argument' (Celsus's) or Ammon's 'pronouncement'; context (Ammon forbade) favours Ammon's word. ἅπαξ: 'simply, once for all'. καὶ κατὰ τὸν Κέλσον, ἢ οὐκ ἄδικά γε: elliptical; 'they do holy things' is understood. Origen paraphrases Darius's question as 'give up this law' (ἀποθέσθαι τοῦτον τὸν νόμον), which differs from Herodotus's wording (burn their fathers); the translation keeps Origen's wording. τοὺς παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις ἀγγέλους πρεσβεύοντας τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ: 'angels who serve as envoys of the things of God' (parallel to Celsus's 'envoy of divine things'); 'God' capitalised as Origen's own term for the true God.

title: The law of nature stands above written law
english: There are, then, two laws set before us in general terms. One is the law of nature, the law God would lay down; the other is the written law in cities. Where the written law does not oppose the law of God, it is right not to trouble the citizens on the pretext of foreign laws. But where the law of nature, that is, of God, commands things contrary to the written law, consider whether reason does not require us to bid a long farewell to what is written and to the intention of the lawgivers, and to give ourselves to God the lawgiver and choose to live according to His word, even if this must be done amid dangers and countless toils, deaths and disgrace.

For it is absurd, when the things that please God are different from those that please some of the laws in cities, and when it is impossible to please both God and those who uphold such laws, to despise the actions by which one will please the Creator of the universe and to choose those by which one will be displeasing to God, but pleasing to laws that are no laws and to their friends. And if in other matters it is reasonable to prefer the law of nature, since it is the law of God, to the law that is written and enacted by men contrary to the law of God, how much more must this be done in the laws that concern God?

So we will not, like the Ethiopians who live around Meroe, worship Zeus and Dionysus alone, as pleases them; no, we will not honour Ethiopian gods in Ethiopian fashion at all. Nor, like the Arabians, will we regard Urania and Dionysus alone as gods; no, we will not regard them as gods at all, gods in whom female and male have been glorified (for the Arabians worship Urania as female and Dionysus as male). Nor will we, like all the Egyptians, hold Osiris and Isis to be gods; nor will we rank Athena with them, as the people of Sais think fit. And if the older people of Naucratis saw fit to revere other objects of worship, while those who began only yesterday or the day before chose to worship Serapis, who never at any time was a god, we will not on that account say, for our part, that there is a new god, one who did not exist before and was not known to men.

For the Son of God, “the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), even if He was seen to have become man only lately, is not for that reason new. For the divine words know Him as the most ancient of all the works of creation, and know that it was to Him that God said concerning the making of man, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26).
translator_notes: ὃν θεὸς ἂν νομοθετήσαι: potential optative, 'the law God would lay down'. κατὰ τὸν τούτου λόγον: 'according to His word' (God's); λόγος could also be 'reason', but the antecedent is God the lawgiver. τοῖς οὐ νόμοις νόμοις: 'laws that are no laws'. The staged Greek prints a bracketed [ὡς] before οἱ τὰ περὶ τὴν Μερόην, which Koetschau deletes; the translation follows the deletion. (δοκοῦντα) after Σαΐταις is an editorial supplement, followed. τὸν οὐ πώποτε γενόμενον θεόν: 'who never at any time was (or became) a god'; Origen denies Serapis divine standing, not historical existence of the cult. εἰ καὶ νεωστὶ ἐνηνθρωπηκέναι ἔδοξεν: ἔδοξεν rendered 'was seen to have become man' rather than 'seemed', to avoid a docetic reading; Origen affirms a real incarnation, and the point is that it appeared to men as recent. πρεσβύτατον αὐτὸν πάντων τῶν δημιουργημάτων: rendered literally 'most ancient of all the works of creation' to keep Origen's own wording; it echoes 'firstborn of all creation' just quoted. Genesis 1:26 quoted from the LXX (κατ᾿ εἰκόνα καὶ ὁμοίωσιν ἡμετέραν; the LXX has καθ᾿ ὁμοίωσιν). The phrase 'dangers and countless toils, deaths and disgrace' may faintly echo 2 Corinthians 11:23–26 (ἐν θανάτοις πολλάκις, κινδύνοις), and the whole paragraph the principle of Acts 5:29; neither is a verbal quotation, so neither is cited inline.

title: Where Celsus’s rule of ancestral worship leads
english: I wish to show how unreasonable Celsus is in saying that each one should worship what is his own and ancestral. He says that the Ethiopians who live at Meroe know only two gods, Zeus and Dionysus, and worship these alone, and that the Arabians likewise know only two, Dionysus, as the Ethiopians do, and Urania, who is their own. By his account, then, the Ethiopians do not worship Urania, nor do the Arabians worship Zeus.

Suppose, then, that an Ethiopian, through some turn of events, finds himself among the Arabians and is thought impious for not worshipping Urania, and on this account is in danger of death. Will it be fitting for the Ethiopian to die, or to act against his ancestral customs and worship Urania? If it will be fitting for him to act against his ancestral customs, he will do what is not holy, so far as Celsus’s arguments go. But if he should be led away to death, let Celsus show what is reasonable about choosing death; for I do not know whether the Ethiopians’ teaching instructs them to reflect as philosophers on the immortality of the soul and on the honour that piety earns, if they worship the gods recognised by their ancestral laws.

The same can be said of the Arabians, if through some turn of events they come to stay among the Ethiopians around Meroe. These too, having been taught to worship only Urania and Dionysus, will not worship Zeus with the Ethiopians; and if, being thought impious, they should be led away to death, let Celsus say what they would reasonably do.

As for the myths about Osiris and Isis, it is needless, and not the right moment, for us to recount them now. And even if the myths are interpreted figuratively, they will teach us to worship lifeless water and the earth that lies beneath men and all animals; for so, I think, they reinterpret Osiris as water and Isis as earth. About Serapis there is a long and conflicting story. He came into public view only yesterday or the day before, through certain sorceries of Ptolemy, who wished to show the people of Alexandria a god, as it were, made manifest. We have read in Numenius the Pythagorean about how he was fashioned, namely that he shares in the substance of all the animals and plants that nature governs. The aim was that, with the help of unhallowed rites and of sorceries that summon demons, he should seem to be fashioned into a god not only by makers of statues but also by magicians and sorcerers, and by the demons charmed by their incantations.
translator_notes: τὴν ἐπὶ θανάτῳ (sc. ὁδόν or δίκην) 'the [road/sentence] to death', rendered 'in danger of death' and 'led away to death'. καθήξει: future of καθήκω, 'will it befit'. The sentence οὐκ οἶδα εἰ τοῦ Αἰθιόπων λόγου ... εἰ (κατὰ) τοὺς πατρίους νόμους σέβοιεν νομιζομένους θεούς is loose: Origen doubts that Ethiopian religion teaches any doctrine of immortality and reward that would make martyrdom for Zeus reasonable; (κατὰ) is an editorial supplement, followed. The bracketed [ἂν] before ἀπάγοιντο is deleted by Koetschau; followed. τροπολογῶνται: 'are interpreted figuratively (allegorised)'. διάφωνος (staged as 'διά φωνος', a spacing break in the TEI): 'conflicting, discordant'. μαγγανείας rendered 'sorceries' (also 'trickeries'); Ptolemy is Ptolemy I Soter, not named further by Origen. Numenius the Pythagorean: the passage is a fragment of Numenius (fr. 53 des Places), cited only by name, not by fragment number inline. ἀτελέστων τελετῶν: an oxymoron, 'rites that initiate into nothing', rendered 'unhallowed rites'. φαρμακῶν taken as from φαρμακός 'sorcerer' (accent as printed); 'demons charmed by their incantations' keeps the Greek agency (the demons are charmed by the magicians' spells and so help make the god). No Scripture in this chapter.

title: Crocodiles, virtue and the second God
english: We must therefore inquire what is fit to be eaten and what is not, in a way that befits a rational and gentle living being that does everything by reason, and not worship sheep or goats or cows arbitrarily. To abstain from these is within reason, for much that is useful comes to human beings from these animals. But to spare even crocodiles, and to hold them sacred to some mythical god, I know not which, how is this not the most foolish thing of all? For it is the mark of people quite out of their senses to spare animals that do not spare, and to cherish animals that feast on human beings.

Yet Celsus is pleased with those who worship and cherish crocodiles according to some ancestral custom, and he has not written a single word against them. It is the Christians who seem to him to deserve blame, though they are taught to loathe vice and to turn away from the works that come from vice, and to revere and honour virtue as begotten by God and as being the Son of God. For we must not suppose that wisdom and righteousness are female in their essence because their names are feminine; and in our teaching these are the Son of God, as his genuine disciple made plain when he said of him: “who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30).

So even if we speak of a second God, let them know that by the second God we mean nothing other than the virtue that contains all virtues, and the Word that contains every rational principle whatever of the things that have come into being according to nature, by primary intent, and for the benefit of the whole. This Word, we say, has been joined to the soul of Jesus as its own and united with it, more closely than with any other soul, since he alone was able to receive perfectly the highest share in the very Word, the very Wisdom and the very Righteousness.
translator_notes: κατὰ ἀποκλήρωσιν ('by allotment') = arbitrarily, as chance assigns, i.e. each nation worshipping whatever animal its custom fell upon; rendered 'as the lot happens to fall'. ἐμβρόντητος ('thunderstruck') = senseless; rendered 'quite out of their senses'. The feminine-noun remark answers the possible objection that Christians, revering ἀρετή/σοφία/δικαιοσύνη (feminine nouns), worship a female power like the goddesses Celsus lists in 5.37-38; the antecedent of ἅπερ (neuter plural) is wisdom and righteousness, and the verb ἐστιν is singular ('which is the Son of God'). 'δεύτερον θεόν' kept as 'a second God', capitalised because Origen means the Son. The λόγος wordplay (the Word containing every λόγος of created things) is kept as 'Word' / 'rational principle'; reviewer: the final λόγον is the head noun of τὸν περιεκτικόν ('the Word that contains ...'), and εἰς χρήσιμον τοῦ παντός goes with γεγενημένων ('made ... for the benefit of the whole'); rendered so. ᾠκειῶσθαι ('made his own, appropriated') and ἡνῶσθαι ('united') rendered as two verbs. γεγενημένην (single ν, from γίνομαι) said of virtue/the Son is kept as 'begotten', since the clause names it the Son of God and the single/double ν spellings are confused in the manuscripts. τῇ Ἰησοῦ supplies ψυχῇ from παρὰ πᾶσαν ψυχήν. αὐτόλογος, αὐτοσοφία, αὐτοδικαιοσύνη rendered 'the very Word, the very Wisdom and the very Righteousness'. 1 Corinthians 1:30 matches the Greek closely (ὃς ἐγενήθη σοφία ἡμῖν ἀπὸ θεοῦ, δικαιοσύνη τε καὶ ἁγιασμὸς καὶ ἀπολύτρωσις).

title: Which law is king of all
english: After saying such things about the different laws, Celsus adds: “Pindar seems to me to have been right when he wrote that law is king of all” (Pindar, fragment 169). Come, then, let us discuss this too. What law, my friend, do you say is king of all? If you mean the laws of the several cities, the statement is false, for not all people are ruled by the same law. In that case it ought to have been said, if at all, “Laws are kings of all,” since over each nation of them all some law is king.

But if you take law in its proper sense, this law is by nature king of all, even if some, like robbers who have revolted from the law, deny it and live like robbers and wrongdoers. We Christians, then, having come to know the law that is by nature king of all, which is the same as the law of God, try to live according to it, and have bidden a long farewell to the laws that are not laws.
translator_notes: Pindar's line νόμος ὁ πάντων βασιλεύς is fragment 169 (Snell-Maehler 169a); it is also quoted by Herodotus 3.38 and Plato, Gorgias 484b. Celsus's sentence is given as a direct quotation (the ὅτι is recitative and μοι is first person). ὦ οὗτος is a brusque address ('you there'), softened to 'my friend' (reviewer: 'my good man' dropped as dated). οἱ κατὰ πόλιν νόμοι = the laws of the individual cities/states. The punctuation of the Perseus text (period after νόμου, then τοῦτον μὲν ἀρνοῦνται) breaks one sentence; it is read as one concessive clause. οὐ νόμοι νόμοι ('laws that are not laws') is an idiom of the type 'a gift that is no gift'. The thought of a law 'by nature' recalls Romans 2:14-15, but there is no verbal echo, so no inline citation is given.

title: Celsus denies that the Jews have anything special
english: Let us also look at what Celsus says next. In it, very little concerns the Christians and most concerns the Jews. He says, then:

“If, then, the Jews were to guard their own law on these grounds, they are not to be blamed for it; rather, those are to be blamed who have abandoned their own ways and taken up those of the Jews. But if they pride themselves on knowing something wiser, and turn away from fellowship with others as not equally pure, they have already heard that not even their doctrine about heaven is their own; but, to pass over everything else, it was held long ago by the Persians too, as Herodotus somewhere shows. ‘For they are accustomed,’ he says, ‘to go up to the highest peaks of the mountains and offer sacrifices to Zeus, calling the whole circle of heaven Zeus’ (Herodotus 1.131). I think, then, that it makes no difference whether one calls Zeus the Most High, or Zen, or Adonai, or Sabaoth, or Amoun, as the Egyptians do, or Papaeus, as the Scythians do.

“Nor, indeed, would they be holier than the others on these grounds: because they are circumcised, for the Egyptians and the Colchians did this before them; nor because they abstain from swine, for the Egyptians do this too, and besides that they abstain from goats and sheep and oxen and fish; and Pythagoras and his disciples abstain from beans, and from everything that has a soul. Nor is it likely that these people are in good standing with God or loved by him in any way differently from the others, or that angels are sent from there to them alone, as though they had been allotted some land of the blessed. For we see what both they and their land have been thought worthy of.

“So let this band depart, having paid the penalty for its boasting. It did not know the great God, but was led astray and deceived by the sorcery of Moses, and it became a pupil of that sorcery to no good end.”
translator_notes: The whole section after 'He says, then' is Celsus's text; it is set in double quotation marks (opening marks at each new paragraph by English convention), with Herodotus's sentence inside it in single marks. Herodotus 1.131 is quoted almost word for word (νομίζουσι Διὶ μὲν ἐπὶ τὰ ὑψηλότατα τῶν ὀρέων ἀναβαίνοντες θυσίας ἔρδειν, τὸν κύκλον πάντα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ Δία καλέοντες). Celsus's other material also draws on Herodotus (circumcision among Egyptians and Colchians, 2.104; Egyptian avoidance of swine, 2.47; Amoun as the Egyptian name of Zeus, 2.42; Papaeus as the Scythian Zeus, 4.59), but he does not quote these, so they are not cited inline. 'κατὰ ταῦτα' refers back to Celsus's principle in 5.25-34 that each nation rightly keeps its ancestral customs. '(ὡς)' is an editorial supplement in the staged text; '(τε)' after βοῶν likewise. The punctuation of the staged text (period before οἷον δή, period before 'ὅτι περιτέμνονται') is followed in sense but joined into English sentences. 'ἐκεῖθεν' ('from there') = from heaven / God's realm; kept literal. ἀλαζονεία rendered 'boasting'; γοητεία 'sorcery'. 'δίκην ὑποσχών' read as 'having paid the penalty' (Celsus probably alludes to the Jewish defeats under Titus and Hadrian, which Origen does not mention here). 'κἀκείνης ... μαθητής': ἐκείνης refers to γοητεία, i.e. a pupil of Moses' sorcery; reviewer changed 'his pupil' to 'a pupil of that sorcery' to keep the Greek referent (Origen's own paraphrase in 5.42, μαθητευθέντων αὐτῷ, is where Moses becomes the teacher). χορός rendered 'band' rather than the stage word 'chorus'. ἔμψυχα rendered 'everything that has a soul' (not 'living things', which would include the beans). τίνων ἠξίωνται has αὐτούς τε καὶ τὴν χώραν as its proleptic subject: 'we see what both they and their land have been thought worthy of'. Δία Ὕψιστον καλεῖν could also be read 'to call the Most High Zeus'; the list of names stands either way, so the literal order is kept. 'Zen' (Ζήν) is a poetic form of the name Zeus. Divine names here are reported names; 'God' is capitalised only in 'the great God' and 'with God', where Celsus speaks of the supreme God.

title: The wise way of life of the Jews
english: It is clear that in these words he accuses the Jews of falsely supposing that they are a chosen portion of the God over all, above all the nations. He charges them, at any rate, with boasting, as people who glory in the great God and yet do not know him, but were led astray by the sorcery of Moses and deceived by him, and became his disciples to no good end.

In part, then, we have already spoken in earlier passages of the venerable and exceptional commonwealth of the Jews, at the time when there stood among them the symbol of the city of God, and of his temple, and of the priestly worship at the temple and the altar. But if anyone fixed his mind on the intention of the lawgiver and on the commonwealth he set up, and examined their life and compared it with the present conduct of the other nations, he would admire no people more, as people who, so far as human beings can, had removed everything that is of no use to the human race and accepted only what is of real use. That is why there were among them no athletic contests, no stage contests, no horse races, and no women selling the bloom of their youth to anyone who wished to sow in vain and to outrage the nature of human seed.

What a thing it was among them to be taught, from their earliest years, to rise above the whole of nature that the senses perceive and never to think that God has his seat anywhere in it, but to seek him above, beyond all bodies! How great a thing that, almost as soon as their reason came into being and reached completion, they were taught the immortality of the soul, the places of judgment beneath the earth, and the honours of those who have lived well! These things were still proclaimed in a more mythical form to children and to those who think as children do. But for those who were already seeking the meaning and wished to advance in it, what had until then been myths, if I may call them so, were transformed into the truth hidden within them.

And I think that, in a manner worthy of their being called the portion of God (Deuteronomy 32:9), they despised all divination, as something that bewitches people to no purpose and that comes from wicked demons rather than from any better nature; and they sought knowledge of what is to come in souls that, because of their utmost purity, had received the Spirit of the God over all.
translator_notes: 'μερίδα θεοῦ' (God's portion) echoes Deuteronomy 32:9 LXX (καὶ ἐγενήθη μερὶς κυρίου λαὸς αὐτοῦ Ιακωβ); cited inline at Origen's own use, not at his paraphrase of Celsus's charge in the first sentence. The staged text puts periods before μετεμορφοῦντο, before ζητεῖν δέ and before δι᾿ ἄκραν; these are read as continuations of the preceding sentences (ζητεῖν depends on νομίζω, parallel to καταπεφρονηκέναι). 'ἐξ ἁπαλῶν ὀνύχων' ('from tender nails') is a Greek proverb for 'from earliest childhood'. 'συμπληρώσει τοῦ λόγου' = the completion of reason (the Stoic notion that reason reaches maturity at a set age); reviewer: γενέσει καὶ συμπληρώσει both govern τοῦ λόγου, so rendered 'as soon as their reason came into being and reached completion' (not 'from birth'). θυμελικοὶ ἀγῶνες = contests held on the stage (music, drama); reviewer changed 'stage shows' to 'stage contests' to keep ἀγῶνες. κατ᾿ αὐτόν (masculine) refers to the lawgiver, not to βούλημα: 'the commonwealth he set up'. πολιτεία rendered 'commonwealth' (not 'polity'); 'still' dropped as not in the Greek (ἡνίκα = 'at the time when'). τὰ ὑπὸ γῆν δικαιωτήρια is a Platonic phrase (cf. Phaedrus 249a) but not a quotation, so not cited; rendered 'places of judgment', τιμάς 'honours'. αἰσθητὴ φύσις rendered 'nature that the senses perceive' to avoid 'sensible' (= reasonable in modern English). The absence of prostitutes may allude to Deuteronomy 23:17 (LXX 23:18), and the rejection of divination to Deuteronomy 18:10-14, but Origen quotes neither, so both are left as possible allusions only. πνεῦμα τοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεοῦ capitalised as 'the Spirit', since Origen means the Holy Spirit who spoke in the prophets.

title: A pattern of the heavenly city
english: As for the rule that one who holds the same beliefs may not be kept a slave for more than six years (Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:12), what need is there to say how reasonable it is, and how it wrongs neither the master nor the slave? So the Jews would not guard their own law on the same grounds as the other nations. For it would be blameworthy in them, and would bring on them a charge of being blind to the superiority of their laws, if they thought these laws had been written in the same way as the others that the nations have.

And even if Celsus does not like it, the Jews do know something wiser, not only than the multitude, but also than those who are thought to be philosophers. For the philosophers, after their solemn discourses in philosophy, sink down to idols and demons, whereas even the least of the Jews looks to the God over all, and to him alone. And so far as this goes, they rightly pride themselves and turn away from fellowship with others as defiled and impious.

Would that they had not sinned by breaking the law, first killing “the prophets” and later plotting against Jesus too (1 Thessalonians 2:15)! Then we would have a pattern of a heavenly city, which Plato too sought to sketch (Plato, Republic 592b). Yet I do not know whether he was able to do as much as Moses and those after him achieved, who nurtured “a chosen race” and “a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9; Exodus 19:6), dedicated to God, on words pure of all superstition.
translator_notes: The six-year limit on slavery for a fellow Hebrew is Exodus 21:2 and Deuteronomy 15:12 (cf. Jeremiah 34:14); Origen paraphrases, so both are cited as allusions. 'τὸν ἀπὸ τῶν αὐτῶν ὁρμώμενον δογμάτων' ('one setting out from the same doctrines') = a fellow member of the same faith, i.e. a fellow Israelite. In this section Origen turns Celsus's own phrases from 5.41 back on him (περιστέλλοιεν τὸν ἴδιον νόμον, μεμπτόν, σοφώτερόν τι εἰδότες, σεμνύνονται, τὴν τῶν ἄλλων κοινωνίαν ἐκτρέπονται); since these are echoes woven into Origen's own sentences rather than fresh quotations, they are not set in quotation marks. The staged text has periods before εἰ νομίζοιεν and before ὅτι οἱ μέν; read as continuations. 'ἀναισθησία' rendered 'being blind to'. 'Killing the prophets' and plotting against Jesus together match 1 Thessalonians 2:15 (τῶν καὶ τὸν κύριον ἀποκτεινάντων Ἰησοῦν καὶ τοὺς προφήτας); cf. Matthew 23:37. 'γένος ἐκλεκτόν' and 'ἔθνος ἅγιον' are from 1 Peter 2:9, which itself draws on Exodus 19:6 (ἔθνος ἅγιον) and Isaiah 43:20 (γένος ἐκλεκτόν). 'A pattern of a heavenly city' that Plato sought to sketch recalls Plato, Republic 9.592b (ἐν οὐρανῷ ἴσως παράδειγμα ἀνάκειται, 'perhaps a pattern is laid up in heaven'), the closing image of Plato's ideal city; the shared terms παράδειγμα and heaven make the reference secure, though Origen may mean the Republic as a whole (διαγράψαι also echoes Republic 500e, the city 'sketched' by painters using the divine pattern). Reviewer: σεμνύνονται rendered 'pride themselves' here and in Celsus's words in 5.41 so the echo shows; 'looks to the God over all, and to him alone' removes the ambiguity of 'the God over all alone'; ὁ ἀπὸ τῶν αὐτῶν ὁρμώμενος δογμάτων rendered 'one who holds the same beliefs' (less stiff than 'comes from').

title: One God, one temple, and the heaven of heavens
english: Since Celsus wants to put the solemn institutions of the Jews on a level with the laws of certain nations, come, let us examine these points too. He thinks, then, that the doctrine about heaven is no different from the doctrine about God, and he says that the Persians, like the Jews, offer sacrifices to Zeus, going up to the highest peaks of the mountains. He does not see that, as the Jews knew one God, so they had one holy house of prayer, one altar for whole burnt offerings, one altar for incense, and one high priest of God.

The Jews, then, had nothing in common with the Persians, who go up to the highest peaks of the mountains, of which there are many, and offer sacrifices that bear no likeness to those under the law of Moses. Under that law the priests of the Jews served “a copy and shadow of the heavenly things” (Hebrews 8:5), and they explained in secret the intention of the law concerning the sacrifices, and of what things these sacrifices were symbols.

So let the Persians call the whole circle of heaven Zeus. We, however, say that heaven is neither Zeus nor God, since we know that even one of the beings lower than God has risen above the heavens and above the whole of nature that the senses perceive. And this is how we understand the words: “Praise God, you heavens of heavens, and the water that is above the heavens; let them praise the name of the Lord” (Psalm 148:4–5).
translator_notes: The staged text has periods after νόμοις, after ἀναβαίνοντας and after ἠπίσταντο that split single sentences; they are read as one argument. θυμιατήριον can mean a censer or the altar of incense (cf. Hebrews 9:4); rendered 'one altar for incense' as the counterpart of the altar of burnt offering. The 'one house, one altar, one high priest' theme reflects the law of the single sanctuary (Deuteronomy 12:5-14) but quotes no verse, so it is not cited inline. 'ὑποδείγματι καὶ σκιᾷ λατρεύουσιν τῶν ἐπουρανίων' is Hebrews 8:5, adapted into past narrative (ἐλάτρευον). Psalm 148:4-5: LXX and English numbering agree for this psalm; the LXX reads αἰνεῖτε αὐτόν ('praise him'), and Origen substitutes τὸν θεόν; rendered as Origen has it. 'τινα τῶν ἡττόνων τοῦ θεοῦ ὑπεραναβεβηκέναι τοὺς οὐρανούς' is singular in the Greek ('someone of those lesser than God'); it probably refers to the soul of Jesus, recalling Hebrews 4:14 (διεληλυθότα τοὺς οὐρανούς) and Ephesians 4:10 (ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν οὐρανῶν), but Origen does not quote either, so they are not cited inline. The singular τινα is kept: 'even one of the beings lower than God has risen'. Reviewer: unaccented τινα could also be neuter plural ('some of the beings lower than God have risen'), e.g. the souls of the saints; the Greek does not settle it, and the singular is kept as the likelier reading with Hebrews 4:14 in view. αἰσθητὴ φύσις rendered 'nature that the senses perceive', as in 5.42.

title: Holy names lose their power in translation
english: But since Celsus thinks it makes no difference whether one calls the Most High Zeus, or Zen, or Adonaeus, or Sabaoth, or Amoun, as the Egyptians do, or Papaeus, as the Scythians do, let us say a little about these matters as well. At the same time we remind the reader of what was said earlier on a question of this kind, when the words of Celsus led us to such subjects.

Now, then, we say again that the nature of names is not a matter of rules laid down by those who give them, as Aristotle thinks (Aristotle, On Interpretation 16a). For the languages spoken among men do not have their origin from men. This is clear to those who are able to attend to the nature of incantations, which, according to the different languages and the different sounds of the names, belong to the fathers of those languages. We treated these things briefly above, where we said that words which by nature have power in a given language no longer accomplish anything when they are translated into another language, as they did in their own sounds.

This is found even in the case of men. Take someone who from his birth has been called by a certain name in the Greek language: if we translated his name into the language of the Egyptians, or of the Romans, or of any other people, we could not make him suffer or do what he would suffer or do if he were called by the name first given to him. Nor, if we translated into Greek the name of someone called from the beginning in the Roman tongue, would we accomplish what the incantation promises to accomplish while it keeps the name first given to him.

If these things said about human names are true, what must we think about the names that, for whatever cause, are referred to the divine? For example, the name Abraham is translated into something in Greek, the name Isaac signifies something, and the word Jacob makes something known. Now if the one who invokes or adjures names “the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:6), he would accomplish this or that, either through the nature of these names or through their power, and demons are overcome and made subject to the one who says them. But if he says, “the God of the chosen father of sound, and the God of laughter, and the God of the supplanter,” what he names does nothing, just like anything else that has no power.

So too, if we translate the name Israel into Greek or into another language, we shall accomplish nothing; but if we keep it, and attach it to the words with which those skilled in these matters have thought fit to join it, then something might happen from that word, as invocations of this kind promise. We shall say the same about the word Sabaoth, which is used in many places in incantations: if we translate the name as “Lord of the powers,” or “Lord of hosts,” or “Almighty” (for those who translate it have rendered it in different ways), we shall accomplish nothing; but if we keep it in its own sounds, we shall accomplish something, as those skilled in these matters say. And we shall say the same about Adonai. If, then, neither Sabaoth nor Adonai accomplishes anything when translated into what they seem to mean in Greek speech, how much less would it do anything, or have any power, among those who think it makes no difference whether one calls the Most High Zeus, or Zen, or Adonaeus, or Sabaoth?
translator_notes: Celsus's list (from 5.41) is given as reported speech ('Celsus thinks'), so it is not set in quotation marks; Δία Ὕψιστον taken as 'call the Most High Zeus' with the following names as alternative predicates. Celsus's form Ἀδωναῖος is kept as 'Adonaeus'; Origen's own Ἀδωναΐ as 'Adonai'. Ζῆνα = Zen, a poetic form of Zeus. Aristotle reference: names are by convention (κατὰ συνθήκην), On Interpretation 2, 16a19-29; Origen discussed this earlier at 1.24. 'The fathers of the languages' (τοῖς πατράσι τῶν διαλέκτων) kept literal; Origen elsewhere links languages to the powers allotted to nations. The etymologies are the traditional ones (Abraham = 'chosen father of sound', Isaac = 'laughter', Jacob = 'supplanter', πτερνιστής, heel-catcher, cf. Genesis 27:36); not cited as Scripture quotations. Koetschau's supplements (τι) and (τῶν ὀνομάτων) are translated. 'Lord of the powers' is the usual LXX rendering of YHWH Sabaoth in the Psalms (e.g. LXX Psalm 23:10 = English Psalm 24:10), 'Almighty' the usual LXX rendering in the prophets; 'Lord of hosts' (στρατιῶν) probably reflects another Greek version (possibly Aquila): not cited inline because Origen names renderings, not verses. Final clause: Greek 'how much more would it do nothing' rendered idiomatically as 'how much less would it do anything'; the subject is the divine name as used by those who treat the names as interchangeable. φωνῆς in 'from such a word' means the spoken name, as with Ἰακὼβ φωνῆς and Σαβαὼθ φωνῆς.

title: Why Christians will not call God Zeus
english: It is because they knew these secret things, and others like them, that Moses and the prophets forbid anyone to speak “the name of other gods” (Exodus 23:13) with a mouth that has learned to pray only to the God over all, or to call them to mind in a heart taught to keep itself pure from all vanity of thoughts and words. And for such reasons we choose to endure every kind of torture rather than confess that Zeus is a god. For we do not suppose that Zeus and Sabaoth are the same; indeed, we do not suppose Zeus to be anything divine at all, but some demon who delights in being called by that name, and who is no friend either to men or to the true God.

And if the Egyptians hold Amoun out to us and threaten us with punishment, we shall die rather than proclaim Amoun a god, a name that is probably used in certain Egyptian incantations that call upon this demon. Let the Scythians, too, say that Papaeus is the God over all; but we shall not be persuaded. We do hold that there is a God over all; but we do not name God by Papaeus as a proper name, as pleases the one who was allotted the Scythian wilderness, together with their nation and their language. For whoever names God by the common word for God, in Scythian or in Egyptian or in any language in which he was brought up, will not sin.
translator_notes: 'The name of other gods' matches LXX Exodus 23:13 (ὄνομα θεῶν ἑτέρων οὐκ ἀναμνησθήσεσθε, οὐδὲ μὴ ἀκουσθῇ ἐκ τοῦ στόματος ὑμῶν), which supplies both 'mouth' and 'call to mind'. Origen says 'Moses and the prophets'; possible further echoes, not cited inline: Joshua 23:7, Psalm 16:4 (LXX 15:4, 'nor will I take their names upon my lips'), Hosea 2:17. 'The one who was allotted the Scythian wilderness' alludes to Origen's view that nations were allotted to angelic powers (cf. LXX Deuteronomy 32:8); not a quotation, so not cited inline. The source punctuation (full stops after θεόν and Παπαῖον, and after ἐντέθραπται) is treated as one continuous sentence in each case; προσηγορικόν = common noun as opposed to a proper name (κύριον ὄνομα). Lower-case 'god' for Zeus and Amoun because Origen denies their divinity (ὁμολογῆσαι θεόν is a predicate, 'confess to be a god'). 'Forbid anyone to speak' renders the bare infinitive ὀνομάζειν after ἀπαγορεύουσιν; μόνῳ goes with θεῷ ('pray only to the God over all').

title: The same rite can have different meanings
english: The reason for the circumcision of the Jews is not the same as the reason for the circumcision of the Egyptians or of the Colchians, and so it could not be thought the same circumcision. Just as one who sacrifices does not sacrifice to the same being, even if he seems to sacrifice in the same way, and one who prays does not pray to the same being, even if he asks for the same things in his prayers, so too, when someone is circumcised, it is not in every case the same as circumcision directed to another. For the purpose, the law and the intention of the one who circumcises make the act different.

To make the point of this subject still clearer, it must be said that the name of justice is the same among all the Greeks; yet it is shown that justice according to Epicurus is one thing; justice according to the Stoics, who deny that the soul has three parts, is another; and justice according to the Platonists, who say that justice is each part of the soul doing its own work, is another again. So too the courage of Epicurus, who endures pains to escape greater pains, is one thing; the courage of the Stoic, who chooses every virtue for its own sake, is another; and courage according to Plato, who says that it is the virtue of the spirited part of the soul and assigns to it a place about the chest, is another again.

In the same way circumcision would differ according to the different doctrines of those who are circumcised. About this it is not necessary to speak now in a work of this kind; whoever wishes to see what moved us on this subject may read what we have written about it in our treatment of Paul's Epistle to the Romans.
translator_notes: Answers Celsus's claim (5.41) that circumcision came from the Egyptians and Colchians. 'Directed to another' renders τῆς πρὸς ἕτερον περιτομῆς, parallel to sacrificing and praying 'to the same' being; οὐδ᾿ ... ἀδιαφορεῖ πάντως ('nor is it in every case no different') is rendered 'not in every case the same', since the argument is that intention, not the act, decides the difference. τὸν τόπον here means the subject under discussion, not a passage. Philosophical references, not quotations, so no inline source given: Platonic justice as each part doing its own work (ἰδιοπραγία), compare Plato, Republic 4.433a-b and 441d-e; spirit lodged in the chest, compare Timaeus 70a. 'Those from Plato' and 'the Stoics' are schools, while for courage the Greek names Plato himself (φάσκοντος agrees with Πλάτωνος). The Romans work is Origen's Commentary on Romans (on Romans 2:25-29); no Scripture verse is quoted here.

title: Circumcision and the hostile angel
english: So if the Jews do take pride in circumcision, they will distinguish it not only from the circumcision of the Colchians and Egyptians but also from that of the Ishmaelite Arabs, although Ishmael was born of their forefather Abraham and was circumcised together with him (Genesis 17:23–26).
