The Jews say that circumcision on the eighth day (Genesis 17:12) is the principal kind, and that circumcision not done in this way comes from force of circumstance.

And perhaps circumcision was performed because of some angel hostile to the Jewish nation, who was able to harm those of them who were not circumcised but was powerless against those who were. Someone will say that this is shown by what is written in Exodus, where before the circumcision of Eliezer the angel was able to act against Moses, but once Eliezer had been circumcised he could do nothing (Exodus 4:24–26). And having learned such things, “Zipporah took a pebble and circumcised” her child (Exodus 4:25). According to the common copies she is recorded as saying, “The blood of my child's circumcision has stopped” (Exodus 4:25–26), but according to the Hebrew, “You are a bridegroom of blood to me” (Exodus 4:25). For she knew the account of this sort of angel, who had power before the blood but ceased because of the blood of circumcision; and for this reason it was said to him, “You are a bridegroom of blood to me.”

But let this much be said, at some risk, about these matters, which seem rather over-curious and not suited to the ears of most people. To them I shall add one more point, as befits a Christian, and then pass on to what follows. For this angel, I think, had power against the uncircumcised among the people, and in a word among all who worshipped the Creator alone; and he had that power for as long as Jesus had not taken a body. But when Jesus had taken one, and His body was circumcised (Luke 2:21), all the angel's power against those circumcised in this worship of God was overthrown; for Jesus brought him down by His unspeakable divinity. That is why His disciples are forbidden to be circumcised, and it is said to them, “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Galatians 5:2).
translator_notes: Source typo ιπερτομῆς read as περιτομῆς. Exodus 4 does not name the son; Origen identifies him as Eliezer (Ἐλιάζαρ in this text; cf. Exodus 18:4), and LXX Exodus 4:24 has 'an angel of the Lord' where the Hebrew has the Lord; 'once Eliezer had been circumcised' clarifies the Greek 'he'. 'Zipporah took a pebble' matches LXX Exodus 4:25 (λαβοῦσα Σεπφωρα ψῆφον περιέτεμεν), which has 'the foreskin of her son' where Origen has 'her child'. The 'common copies' reading ἔστη τὸ αἷμα τῆς περιτομῆς τοῦ παιδίου μου is the LXX of Exodus 4:25 and 4:26; ἔστη taken as 'has stopped' (stanched). The Hebrew 'bridegroom of blood' is Exodus 4:25 (Hebrew; also 4:26). 'Said to him' is ambiguous in the Greek (the angel or Moses); kept ambiguous. Doubtful sense: 'all his power against those circumcised in this worship of God' translates the transmitted περιτεμνομένων; the argument might seem to want 'uncircumcised', but the text as given is translated without emendation. 'His' in 'His unspeakable divinity' added for English sense (ἀφάτῳ θειότητι). Galatians 5:2 quoted closely (Origen adds ὅτι). κατὰ τῶν μὴ περιτεμνομένων ἀπὸ τοῦ λαοῦ καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς πάντων τῶν σεβόντων: πάντων τῶν σεβόντων taken with ἀπό, parallel to τοῦ λαοῦ, so the angel's power is over the uncircumcised among all worshippers of the Creator (not over all such worshippers); this fits the claim that he was powerless against the circumcised. κἄν at the start of the chapter read as 'if' (the Jews do take pride), not concessive.

title: Abstaining from food for the right reason
english: Nor do the Jews take pride in abstaining from swine as if it were some great thing. Their pride is rather that, having learned the nature of clean and unclean animals, they know the reason for the distinction and that the swine is ranked among the unclean (Leviticus 11:7). These things, too, were symbols of certain realities until the coming of Jesus. After Him it was said to His disciple, who did not yet understand the meaning of these things and said, “Nothing common or unclean has entered my mouth” (Acts 11:8), “What God has cleansed, you must not call common” (Acts 10:15).

So it is nothing to the Jews or to us that the priests of the Egyptians abstain not only from swine but also from goats, sheep, oxen and fish. But since “it is not what enters the mouth that defiles a man” (Matthew 15:11), and “food will not commend us to God” (1 Corinthians 8:8), we do not think highly of ourselves for not eating, nor do we come to eating out of gluttony. Therefore, so far as we are concerned, let the followers of Pythagoras, who abstain from living things, go their way.

But notice the difference between the reason why the followers of Pythagoras abstain from living things and the reason why the ascetics among us do so. They abstain from living things because of the myth about the soul passing from one body into another: “And who will lift up his dear son and slay him with a prayer, the great fool?” (Empedocles, fragment 137 Diels–Kranz). But if we do such a thing, we do it because we discipline “the body” and bring it into subjection (1 Corinthians 9:27), and wish to put to death “the members that are on the earth: fornication, uncleanness, licentiousness, passion, evil desire” (Colossians 3:5); and we do everything so that we may put to death “the deeds of the body” (Romans 8:13).
translator_notes: Swine as unclean: Leviticus 11:7 (also Deuteronomy 14:8). Peter's words 'entered my mouth' match Acts 11:8 (Acts 10:14 has 'I have never eaten'); the reply 'what God has cleansed' is Acts 10:15, repeated at Acts 11:9. Matthew 15:11 quoted with the plural τὰ εἰσερχόμενα; 'commend' renders παραστήσει in 1 Corinthians 8:8. The line on the slain son is Empedocles, Purifications (DK 31 B137), here adapted as a question with future σφάξει. 1 Corinthians 9:27 quoted in first person plural. Colossians 3:5 as quoted adds ἀσέλγειαν ('licentiousness'), which is not in the standard text of that verse (compare Galatians 5:19); translated as Origen gives it. χαιρόντων rendered 'let them go their way' (polite dismissal), not a wish of joy. 'Living things' = ἔμψυχα, animal food.

title: God’s favour passes from the Jews to the Gentiles
english: Pronouncing further on the Jews, Celsus says: “Nor is it likely that they stand in good repute with God, or are loved by Him in any way differently from others, or that angels are sent from there to them alone, as though they had been allotted some land of the blessed; for we see what they and their land have been thought worthy of.”

We shall refute this too. We say that this nation's good standing with God is shown also by the fact that the God over all is called the God of the Hebrews even by those who are strangers to our faith. And because they stood in good repute, so long as they were not forsaken, they continued to be guarded by divine power, though they were few in number. So it was that not even under Alexander of Macedon did they suffer anything at his hands, although, because of certain agreements and oaths, they had refused to take up arms against Darius. At that time, they say, when the high priest of the Jews had put on his priestly robe, Alexander even bowed down before him, saying that he had seen someone in this very dress who promised him “in his sleep” that he would make the whole of Asia subject to him (see Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 11.8.5).

We Christians, then, say that standing in good repute with God, and being loved in a way different from others, did indeed belong to them in full. But we say that this dispensation and the grace have passed over to us, since Jesus moved the power that was among the Jews to those from the Gentiles who believed in Him. That is why the Romans, though they wished to do much against the Christians to stop them existing any longer, have not been able to do so; for a divine hand was fighting for them, wishing to sow the word of God from one corner, the land of Judea, through the whole race of mankind.
translator_notes: Source typo δυνάμενως read as δυνάμεως. Celsus's sentence 'we see them and the land, of what (τίνων) they have been deemed worthy' read as a prolepsis and rendered 'we see what they and their land have been thought worthy of' (ironic: their ruin). The passive 'the high priest ... was bowed down to by Alexander' recast with Alexander as subject; agency unchanged. τῶν ἐθνῶν rendered 'the Gentiles'. 'Called the God of the Hebrews even by strangers to our faith' probably refers to pagan invocations (compare Exodus 3:18, 'the God of the Hebrews', but no quotation is made, so not cited inline). The Alexander story (high priest Jaddua, refusal to break oaths to Darius, Alexander's dream) is in Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 11.8.3-5 (about 11.317-339); Koetschau marks 'in his sleep' (κατὰ τοὺς ὕπνους) as a quoted phrase; Origen says only 'they say'. Crux: φάσκοντος ὦφθαι αὐτῷ τούτῳ τῷ σχήματι † ἑωρακέναι τινά doubles the verb ('appeared' / 'had seen'); translated by the clear sense, 'he had seen someone in this very dress'. '(αὐ)τῷ Ἰησοῦ': Koetschau's supplement gives πιστεύσαντας αὐτῷ, with the genitive Ἰησοῦ as subject of μεταστήσαντος, hence 'since Jesus moved the power ... to those who believed in Him'. 'The word of God' here is the message preached, so lower-case 'word'. Section 51 continues to Celsus's charges against Moses and the Christians.

title: We commend the Teacher, not ourselves
english: But since we have answered, as far as we could, what Celsus set out in accusing the Jews and their teaching, come, let us set out what follows and show that we are not boasting when we profess to know the great God, and that we have not been led astray, as Celsus thinks, by the sorcery of Moses, or even of our Saviour Jesus himself. Rather, it is for a good end that we listen to the God made known in Moses and have received Jesus as the Son of God, Jesus to whom that God bears witness as God, hoping for the best when we live according to his word.

We shall willingly refrain from speaking about what we set out earlier, when we taught where we have come from, whom we have as our founder, and what law comes from him. And if Celsus would have it that we differ in nothing from the Egyptians who worship the goat, or the ram, or the crocodile, or the ox, or the hippopotamus, or the dog-headed baboon, or the cat, that is for him to know, and for anyone who shares his opinion on this. For our part, we have defended at length in what came before, as far as we were able, the honour we give to Jesus, showing that we have found something better. And when we alone declare that the truth, pure and unmixed with falsehood, is found in the teaching of Jesus Christ, we are commending not ourselves but the Teacher, to whom the God over all has borne witness in many ways: both by the prophetic words among the Jews and by the plain evidence itself. For it is shown that he could not have done such great things without God.
translator_notes: τοῦ ἐν Μωϋσεῖ θεοῦ ἀκούομεν, literally 'we hear the God in Moses', is rendered 'the God made known in Moses' (Moses standing for his books). τὸν μαρτυρούμενον ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ θεὸν Ἰησοῦν ὡς υἱὸν θεοῦ: θεόν is taken as predicate of μαρτυρούμενον ('witnessed by him as God'), then 'as Son of God'. μόνοι ἡμεῖς is nominative and goes with 'we' ('we alone declare'), not with the teaching. The staged text punctuates with full stops after ἐκκείμενα, γοητείᾳ and ἐξεθέμεθα; these are read as running on into the following clauses. The animal list repeats Celsus's charge from earlier in the book; κυνοκέφαλος is the sacred baboon. No Scripture quoted; ὁ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεός is Origen's usual title and is not marked as an allusion to Romans 9:5. Review: ὡς υἱὸν θεοῦ goes with παρεδεξάμεθα ('received Jesus as the Son of God'), so it now stands with 'received'; ἐπάν rendered 'when' (not 'if'); ὑπήχθημεν 'led astray'. οὐκ ἀθεεί is a Homeric turn of phrase Origen uses often; not cited.

title: Celsus asks whether Jesus was the only angel
english: The passage of Celsus that we now wish to examine runs as follows: “And indeed we pass over all the points on which they are refuted about their teacher. Let him be taken to be truly an angel. But did he come first and alone, or did others come before him too? If they should say that he alone came, they would be convicted of lying and contradicting themselves. For they say that others too have often come, and indeed sixty or seventy together; that these became wicked and are punished by being put in bonds in the earth; and that this is why the hot springs are their tears. What is more, they say that an angel came to the very tomb of this man (some say one, others two), the ones who answered the women that he had risen (Matthew 28:5–6; Luke 24:4–6). For the child of God, it seems, could not open the tomb, but needed someone else to move the rock away (Matthew 28:2).

“Again, concerning Mary when she was with child, an angel came to the carpenter (Matthew 1:20), and another angel came so that they might snatch up the baby and flee (Matthew 2:13). And why need one go through everything in detail and count up those said to have been sent to Moses and to others of theirs? If, then, others too were sent, it is clear that this one also was sent by the same God. But let him be taken, if you like, to bring some greater message, as though the Jews were doing wrong, or debasing piety, or doing unholy things; for this is what they hint at.”
translator_notes: The whole chapter after the first sentence is Celsus's own wording and stands in double quotation marks. The infinitives from ἐλθεῖν γάρ onward depend on λέγουσι ('they say'), so 'they say' is kept for the tomb clause. δοκείτω τις ὡς ἀληθῶς ἄγγελος is rendered 'Let him be taken to be truly an angel' (τις softens: 'a sort of angel'). The 'sixty or seventy' angels bound in the earth and the hot springs as their tears do not match the extant Book of Enoch (1 Enoch 6–10 has two hundred watchers bound under the earth); Origen in 5.54–55 says Celsus misheard Enoch. No inline citation for 'sent to Moses and to others': too general to pin to one verse (possible Exodus 3:2; 23:20). The closing charge that the Jews were 'doing wrong ... doing unholy things' is answered by Origen in 5.58 with Matthew 21:41; here it is Celsus's paraphrase of Christian claims and is not cited. ἐξαρπάσαντας is plural (Joseph and Mary). παραχαραττόντων: to debase coinage; 'debasing piety'. Review: τοὺς ἀποκρινομένους is an attributive participle, not purpose ('the ones who answered', not 'to answer'); ὁμοῦ 'together' to match 5.54–55; ὅδε παρὰ τοῦ αὐτοῦ θεοῦ supplies ἐπέμφθη from the protasis ('was sent by').

title: The Angel of Great Counsel
english: What we said earlier, in the parts where we dealt separately with our Saviour Jesus Christ in reply to Celsus's statements, would have been enough. But so that we may not seem to pass over any passage of his writing on purpose, as though we could not answer it, come, even if we are going to repeat ourselves, since Celsus challenges us to it, let us treat the matter as briefly as we can, and see whether anything clearer or newer on the same matters occurs to us.

He says, then, that he passes over all the points on which Christians are refuted about their teacher, though he has passed over nothing that he could say, as is clear from what he said earlier; he does this merely by following a rhetorical device. But that we are not refuted about so great a Saviour as ours, even if our accuser seems to refute us, will be clear to those who read closely, with a love of truth, all that was prophesied and recorded about him.

Next, since he is thought to be speaking by way of concession when he says of the Saviour, “Let this man be taken to be truly an angel,” we say that we do not take this as something Celsus concedes; we take it from looking at the work of him who has visited the whole human race with his own word and teaching, as far as each of those who received him had room for it. That was the work of one who was not simply an angel but, as the prophecy about him named him, the Angel “of great counsel” (Isaiah 9:6). For he announced to men the great counsel of God, the Father of all things, concerning them: that those who yield to it by living in pure godliness are going up to God through great deeds, while those who do not receive him are putting themselves far from God (Psalm 73:27) and travelling toward destruction through their unbelief concerning God.

Then next he says: “Even if this man came to men as an angel, did he come first and alone, or did others come before him too?” And he thinks he meets each alternative at length, though no one who is truly a Christian says that Christ alone has visited the human race. And Celsus says that others too have appeared to men: “If they should say that he alone …”
translator_notes: Isaiah 9:6 in English Bibles = LXX Isaiah 9:5 (μεγάλης βουλῆς ἄγγελος, a reading found only in the Septuagint). Origen plays on ἄγγελος / ἤγγελλε ('angel' / 'announced'); the pun cannot be kept in English. Psalm 73:27 = LXX Psalm 72:27 (οἱ μακρύνοντες ἑαυτοὺς ἀπὸ σοῦ ἀπολοῦνται): ἑαυτοὺς μακρυνόντων ... ἐπὶ τὴν ἀπώλειαν matches both the verb and the outcome, so it is cited as a clear allusion. ὡς ἕκαστος ἐχώρει may echo Matthew 19:11–12 (χωρεῖν) but is not cited. εἰκόντων ... τῷ βιοῦν: τῷ βιοῦν taken as the dative object of εἴκω ('give themselves to living'). The last sentence is broken in the staged text: (γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων·) is an editorial supplement, and καὶ ἄλλους ὦφθαί φησιν ... εἰ μὲν δὴ φαῖεν ὅτι μόνος seems to give Celsus's opening words of his first alternative (compare 5.52), so they are printed as a broken-off quotation. The quoted 'Even if this man came ...' differs slightly from Celsus's wording in 5.52; Origen is restating it. Text has οτι (unaccented) before δοκείτω; read ὅτι introducing the quotation. Review: εἰκόντων ... τῷ βιοῦν is now read as 'yielding (to the counsel) by living', τῷ βιοῦν as dative of means, in contrast with μὴ προσιεμένων ('not receiving'); the earlier note's 'give themselves to living' is withdrawn. τῷ δ᾿ ἔργῳ αὐτοῦ ἐνορῶντες depends on λαμβάνομεν ('we take it from looking at his work'), so the second sentence is joined back to the first. ἐὰν ἄρα τι ὑποπέσῃ: 'and see whether anything ... occurs' (the old 'in case' could read as 'to prevent'). Isaiah 9:6 (LXX 9:5) and Psalm 73:27 (LXX 72:27) checked against the LXX wording.

title: Who says he came alone
english: Then he answers himself as he pleases. But in fact Christ is not recorded as the only one to have visited the human race. So true is this that even those who, using the teaching of the name of Jesus as a pretext, have turned away from the Creator as lesser and gone over to some God as greater and as Father of the one who came, say that even before him some visited the human race from the Creator.

But since we are examining this passage with a love of truth, we will say that Apelles, the disciple of Marcion, who became the father of a certain heresy and regarded the writings of the Jews as myth, says that this one alone has visited the human race. So not even against him, though he says that Jesus alone has come from God to men, could Celsus reasonably bring the argument that others too have come; for, as we said before, Apelles does not believe the Jewish Scriptures, which report rather marvellous things. Much less will he accept what Celsus seems to have set down after mishearing what is written in Enoch.

No one, then, convicts us of lying and of asserting contradictory things, as though we said both that our Saviour alone came and that many others have often come. But in his inquiry into the angels who have come to men, Celsus sets down in great confusion what reached him indistinctly from what is written in Enoch. He does not appear even to have read these writings, nor to have known that in the churches the books inscribed with Enoch's name are not generally received as divine. That is why he might be thought to have tossed out the claim that sixty or seventy came down together, having become wicked.
translator_notes: οὕτω δ᾿ οὐ μόνος ἱστόρηται ἐπιδεδημηκέναι: the subject is unexpressed; 'Christ' (from the end of 5.53) is supplied. ὡς καὶ τοὺς ... φάσκειν is consecutive ('so that even those ... say'), rendered 'So true is this that even those ...'. The group described (who left the Creator for a higher God and Father of Jesus) are Marcionite-type teachers; Origen names Apelles, Marcion's disciple, as the exception who says Jesus alone came. ὅτι τε μόνος ἦλθεν ... καὶ ὅτι, ἐπεὶ ἄλλοι πολλοὶ πολλάκις ἐληλύθασι is corrupt in the staged text (ἐπεί has no clause to govern); rendered by sense 'both that ... and that many others have often come'. οὐ πάνυ φέρεται ὡς θεῖα may mean 'by no means received' or more softly 'not generally received'; the review gives the softer sense, since Origen himself cites Enoch elsewhere with reserve ('if anyone accepts the book') and so does not treat it as wholly rejected. The staged text has full stops after γράμματα and ἀπιστοῦντα that break single sentences; read as running on. Enoch is not Scripture for this edition, so no inline citation is given; the 'sixty or seventy' is Celsus's figure, not in extant 1 Enoch. Review: the closing τὸ ... καταβεβηκέναι, κακοὺς γενομένους is Origen's restatement (Celsus wrote ἐλθεῖν in 5.52), so it is no longer printed in quotation marks; ἐῤῥιφέναι 'tossed out' (the old 'at random' was an addition). 'by saying both' made the clause read as if the accuser said both; now 'as though we said both'. ἐλάττονος 'lesser' (not 'an inferior being'); ὡς governs both 'greater' and 'Father'.

title: The sons of God and the tears of angels
english: But let us be more generous and grant him what he did not see in what is written in Genesis, that “the sons of God, seeing that the daughters of men were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all whom they chose” (Genesis 6:2). Even so, we shall persuade those who can hear the intention of prophecy that about these things too one of those before us referred these words to the teaching about souls, souls that had come to desire the life of men in the body; and he said, interpreting figuratively, that this is what is meant by “daughters of men.” Yet however things may stand with the sons of God who desired the daughters of men, the passage does nothing to help Celsus show that Jesus was not the only one to have visited men as an angel, Jesus, who has plainly become the Saviour and benefactor of all who turn away from the flood of wickedness.

Then, mixing up and confusing what he heard, however he heard it, and things written wherever they were written, whether held by Christians to be divine or not, he says that the sixty or seventy who came down together are punished by being put in bonds in the earth. And he cites as from Enoch, though without naming him, the words “that is why the hot springs are their tears,” a thing neither said nor heard in the churches of God. For no one was so foolish as to give the angels who came down from heaven bodily tears like those of men. And if we must jest in answer to what Celsus labours at so earnestly against us, it must be said that no one would have called the hot springs, most of which are sweet, the tears of the angels, since the nature of tears is salty; unless, of course, Celsus's angels weep sweet tears.
translator_notes: Genesis 6:2 is quoted in the Septuagint wording (ἰδόντες ... οἱ υἱοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ τὰς θυγατέρας τῶν ἀνθρώπων ὅτι καλαί εἰσιν ...). 'One of those before us' is unnamed; the soul-reading matches Philo, On the Giants 6–18, but Origen does not name him, so this is a probable identification only. ἅπερ τροπολογῶν ἔφασκε λελέχθαι 'θυγατέρας ἀνθρώπων': ἅπερ is neuter plural with a vague antecedent (human bodies or bodily life); rendered 'this is what is meant'. The staged text has a stray raised point in τοῦ· ἐν σώματι, ignored. υἱοὺς θεῶν ('sons of gods') in the staged text is rendered 'sons of God' to match the Genesis quotation just given; θεῶν may be a slip for θεοῦ, or Origen may echo Celsus's pagan idiom; flagged as a doubtful reading. γλυκεῖαι: 'sweet' (fresh) water, kept as 'sweet' for both clauses to keep Origen's joke. χύσις τῆς κακίας: 'flood' (pouring-out) of wickedness. Full stops after γεγραμμένων and ἦν in the staged text break single sentences; read as running on. Review: Genesis 6:2 checked against the LXX wording (exact). 'ever' dropped (not in οὐδὲ ... ἦν); σωματοποιήσῃ ... ἐν τοῖς ... ἀγγέλοις recast in natural order; ψυχῶν ... γενομένων made explicit as the souls that desired bodily life. The υἱοὺς θεῶν reading stays flagged; the owner may wish to check Koetschau's apparatus.

title: One angel at the tomb, or two
english: Then next, mixing things that do not mix and making alike things that are unlike, he adds to his story of the sixty or seventy angels who, as he says, came down and, according to him, wept springs of hot water, that two angels are reported by some to have come to the tomb of Jesus himself, and one by others. He did not notice, I think, that Matthew and Mark reported one (Matthew 28:2–5; Mark 16:5), and Luke and John two (Luke 24:4; John 20:12). These accounts were not contradictory. For those who recorded one say that this was the one who rolled away “the stone” from the tomb (Matthew 28:2); while the others say that the two are those who, “in dazzling clothing” (Luke 24:4), stood by the women who had come to the tomb, or those who were seen inside “sitting in white” (John 20:12).

To show now that each of these is both possible and actually happened, and that it points to a figurative meaning about the things that appear beforehand to those prepared to behold the resurrection of the Word, does not belong to the present treatise but rather to commentaries on the Gospel.
translator_notes: Celsus is reported in indirect speech here, so his words are not in quotation marks; the quoted phrases are Gospel wording: τὸν λίθον (Matthew 28:2 ἀπεκύλισε τὸν λίθον), ἐν ἐσθῆτι ἀστραπτούσῃ (Luke 24:4, exact), ἐν λευκοῖς καθεζομένους (John 20:12, exact). In Mark 16:5 the one figure is a 'young man' sitting inside; Mark does not say he rolled the stone, so Origen's 'those who recorded one say this was the one who rolled away the stone' fits Matthew most exactly. The staged text has a full stop after λόγῳ that breaks the sentence; read as running on. τοῦ λόγου with ἀνάστασιν taken as 'the Word' (Christ), capitalised. πηγὰς θερμῶν: 'springs of hot water' (θερμῶν, neuter plural, 'hot waters'). Review: the phrase 'in dazzling clothing' was placed so that it seemed to describe the women; it now stands with the two angels. οἱ δὲ τοὺς δύο ... is parallel to τοῦτόν φασιν εἶναι ('say that the two are those who ...'). δυνατὸν καὶ γεγενημένον καὶ δηλωτικόν: read with the first draft as three predicates of ἕκαστον ('possible, actually happened, and points to'); 'it would be possible now to show that each both happened and points to ...' is the alternative reading. All Gospel phrases checked: Matthew 28:2 (ἀπεκύλισε τὸν λίθον), Luke 24:4, John 20:12 exact; Mark 16:5 one young man.

title: Marvels told by Greeks and by Christians
english: That marvellous things have at times appeared to men has been reported among the Greeks too, not only by those who might be suspected of making up myths, but also by those who have given great proof that they pursue philosophy genuinely and set out truthfully what has come down to them. We have read such things in Chrysippus of Soli, and some in Pythagoras, and also in some more recent writers who lived only yesterday or the day before, such as Plutarch of Chaeronea in his work On the Soul and Numenius the Pythagorean in the second book of On the Incorruptibility of the Soul.

Or is it that when Greeks tell such things, and above all those among them who are philosophers, what they say is no matter for mockery or laughter, nor fictions and myths; but when those who are devoted to the God of all things, and who, rather than speak a falsehood about God even in a word, undergo every outrage even to death, report appearances of angels as eyewitnesses, they are judged unworthy of belief and their words are not ranked among things that are true? But it is not reasonable to judge in this way who speaks the truth and who lies. For those who train themselves not to be deceived pronounce slowly and with caution, after much exact inquiry and examination of each matter, that these men tell the truth and those men lie in the marvels they report; since not all show themselves worthy of belief, nor are all clearly proved to have handed down fictions and myths to mankind.

Further, about the resurrection of Jesus from the dead this too must be said: that at that time one angel or two should have been seen announcing that he had been raised (Matthew 28:6; Luke 24:4–6) and that he cares for those who believe this for their own benefit, is no wonder. But that at all times those who believe in this way that Jesus has been raised, and who show as no small fruit of their faith a vigorous life and a change from the flood of evils, are not without angels who take hold of them and help them in their turning to God, does not seem to me unreasonable.
translator_notes: The works named are Origen's own references: Plutarch, On the Soul (lost; fragments survive), and Numenius, On the Incorruptibility of the Soul, book 2 (lost); no further source is given. Chrysippus and Pythagoras are named without a work. ἐν τοῖς περὶ ψυχῆς, plural, may mean 'in his books On the Soul'. βράδιον in the staged text is taken as βραδέως / βράδιον ('slowly'). [τῶν] before ἐναργῶς is bracketed by the editor and ignored. μηδὲ μέχρι φωνῆς: 'not even as far as speech', rendered 'even in a word'. ἀεί is taken with the whole clause ('at all times ... are never without angels'). Origen again plays on ἄγγελον / ἀγγέλλοντα ('angel' / 'announcing'). The angel's announcement 'he has been raised' alludes to the resurrection narratives (ἠγέρθη, Matthew 28:6; Luke 24:6), cited inline as a clear allusion. οὐκ εὐκαταφρόνητον rendered 'no small' (literally 'not easily despised'). Review: ἀεί was attached in English to 'believe'; it now heads the clause ('But that at all times ...'), keeping the τότε μέν / ἀεὶ δέ contrast. ἕνα ἢ δεύτερον 'one angel or two'. ἐρρωμένον 'vigorous'. κατὰ τοὺς τόπους 'each matter' (not textual 'passages'). προνοεῖσθαι is read with αὐτόν (the risen Jesus cares for believers); it could instead go with ὦφθαι (the angel provides for them); the sense is close either way.

title: The angel who rolled away the stone
english: Celsus also finds fault with the account which says that an angel rolled away “the stone” (Matthew 28:2) from the tomb where the body of Jesus lay. He goes about it like a schoolboy who has been set, as a classroom exercise, to accuse someone from the stock headings of rhetoric. And as though he had hit upon something clever against the account, he says: “The child of God, it seems, could not open the tomb, but needed someone else to move the rock away.”

I do not want to labour over the details of the passage, nor to seem to philosophize out of season by setting out a figurative interpretation at this point. So I will speak of the narrative itself. On its face it appears more dignified that the lesser one, the servant, should have rolled away “the stone” than that he who was rising for the benefit of human beings should have done it himself. Not to mention that those who plotted against the Word, who wanted to kill him and to show everyone that he was dead and nothing at all, wanted his tomb never to be opened, so that no one might see the Word alive after their plot. But the angel of God, who comes for the salvation of human beings as fellow worker of the Angel, is stronger than the plotters and rolls away the heavy stone. He does this so that those who think the Word is dead may be persuaded that he “is not among the dead” (Luke 24:5–6) but lives and “goes before” (Matthew 28:7) those who wish to follow him. And he goes before them in order to show them what follows on from what he showed them earlier, when, in the first stage of their instruction, they could not yet take in things greater than those.

Then, after this, he somehow throws in, though I do not know what use he thinks it serves his purpose, the story that an angel came to Joseph about Mary when she was with child (Matthew 1:20), and again an angel came so that they would snatch away the newborn child, who was being plotted against, and flee into Egypt (Matthew 2:13). We have already discussed these matters above, in answer to what he said.

And what is Celsus driving at with the fact that the Scriptures record angels being sent to Moses and to the others? It seems to me to contribute nothing to what he wants, especially since none of those angels contended on behalf of the human race to turn it, as far as was possible, from its sins. Grant, then, that others too were sent from God. Let this one proclaim something more. And since the Jews were going astray, debasing true religion, and doing what is unholy, let him hand over the kingdom of God to “other farmers” (Matthew 21:41, 43): to those who everywhere in the churches keep watch over themselves and do everything they can, by a pure life and by words that agree with that life, to bring to the God of all the starting points they have drawn from the teaching of Jesus.
translator_notes: Celsus's mocking sentence is printed as a quotation; the rest is Origen. 'τοπικῶς' = arguing from rhetorical topoi (stock headings), rendered as a schoolroom exercise. 'οὐ λέγω δ᾿ ὅτι' is a praeteritio (he says the thing while saying he does not), rendered 'Not to mention that'. The phrase 'ὁ δὲ ὑπὲρ σωτηρίας ἀνθρώπων ἐπιδημῶν συνεργὸς τοῦ ἀγγέλου ἄγγελος θεοῦ' is difficult: the subject is the angel of God at the tomb; 'fellow worker of the angel' most likely refers to Christ under the title 'Angel' (compare the LXX 'Angel of great counsel', Isaiah 9:5 LXX = Isaiah 9:6 English), so 'Angel' is capitalized; the text may also be faulty here (one might expect τοῦ λόγου). No inline citation is given for that uncertain allusion. 'οὐκ ἔστι μετὰ τῶν νεκρῶν' blends Luke 24:5 ('Why do you seek the living among the dead?') with 24:6 ('he is not here'); 'προάγει' is the angel's message in Matthew 28:7 (also Mark 16:7). 'τοῖς μὴ χωροῦσί πω αὐτῶν μείζονα' taken as 'things greater than these (αὐτῶν), which they could not yet take in'. 'Μωϋσεῖ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις' is read as dative of recipients (angels sent to Moses and the others); it could also be dative of agent ('recorded by Moses and the others'). 'ἐκείνων' (none of those) is taken as those earlier messengers. The imperatives πεπέμφθωσαν / ἀπαγγελλέτω / μεταδεδωκέτω are concessive-hortatory ('Grant... let him'). 'ἄλλοις γεωργοῖς' quotes Matthew 21:41; the handing over of the kingdom echoes 21:43. The final clause (bringing the ἀφορμαί from Jesus's teaching to God) is rendered literally; the object of προσαγαγεῖν is the starting points themselves.

title: What we hold in common with the Jews
english: Next Celsus says: “So the same God belongs to the Jews and to these people,” plainly meaning the Christians. And as if he were drawing a conclusion that would never be conceded, he says this: “Clearly so, since those of the great church admit this, and accept as true the account of the world’s making that is current among the Jews, at least about the six days and the seventh.” On that seventh day, as Scripture says, God “ceased from his works” (Genesis 2:2), withdrawing into his own exalted contemplation. But according to Celsus, who neither attended to what is written nor understood it, God “rested,” which is not written. About the making of the world, and the Sabbath rest that remains after it for the people of God (Hebrews 4:9), there would be “much to say,” and it would be mystical and deep and “hard to explain” (Hebrews 5:11).

Then, wanting to fill out his book and to make it look large, he seems to me to add certain things at random, such as the matter of the first man: that we say he is the same man the Jews speak of, and that we trace the line of descent from him in the same way they do. But we know of no plotting of brothers against one another. We know that Cain plotted against Abel (Genesis 4:8), and Esau against Jacob (Genesis 27:41); but Abel did not plot against Cain, nor Jacob against Esau. Had that happened, Celsus would have been right to say that we tell the same stories as the Jews about brothers plotting against one another.

Grant too that we speak, as they do, of the same going down into Egypt (Genesis 46:6) and of the return from there (Exodus 12:41), and not of a flight, as Celsus supposes. What, then, do these things contribute to the charge against us or against the Jews? Where he thought he would mock us in the account of the Hebrews, he called it a flight. But where the real business was to examine the scourges which are recorded to have come upon Egypt from God (Exodus 7:14–12:30), that he deliberately passed over in silence.
translator_notes: Attribution: 'οὐκοῦν ὁ αὐτὸς θεὸς Ἰουδαίοις τε καὶ τοῖσδε' is Celsus; 'δῆλον δ᾿ ὅτι τοῖς Χριστιανοῖς' is Origen's gloss. The words after 'τοῦτό φησι·' ('σαφῶς γε τῶν ἀπὸ μεγάλης ἐκκλησίας... τῆς ἑβδόμης') are taken as Celsus's own, so 'the great church' is Celsus's phrase (contrasted with the sects he lists in 5.61-62); it is possible to read 'σαφῶς γε...' instead as Origen's retort ('though plainly those of the great church admit it'), so the boundary of the quotation is uncertain. Origen contrasts Scripture's κατέπαυσεν ('ceased', Genesis 2:2 LXX 'κατέπαυσεν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἑβδόμῃ ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν ἔργων αὐτοῦ') with Celsus's ἀναπαυσάμενος ('rested'); the English keeps the two verbs distinct. 'περιωπή' (literally a lookout or high vantage point) is used by Origen of God's contemplation; rendered 'exalted contemplation'. Hebrews 4:9 (σαββατισμὸς ἀπολείπεται τῷ λαῷ τοῦ θεοῦ) and Hebrews 5:11 (πολὺς ἡμῖν ὁ λόγος καὶ δυσερμήνευτος) are woven into Origen's sentence. Celsus evidently claimed Christians share the Jewish stories of brothers plotting against each other; Origen denies that the plots were mutual. The descent into Egypt and the Exodus are narrative references, cited at Genesis 46:6 and Exodus 12:41; the plagues are cited as the whole plague narrative (Exodus 7:14–12:30).

title: The veil over the reading of Moses
english: If we must answer Celsus precisely, since he thinks that we hold the same opinions as the Jews on the matters set out, we will say this. We both agree that the books were written by the divine Spirit; but about the interpretation of what is in the books we no longer say the same things. We do not even live as the Jews do, because we judge that the literal interpretation of the laws is not the one that contains the intention of the legislation.

And we say that “whenever Moses is read, a veil lies upon the heart” (2 Corinthians 3:15), because the intention of the law of Moses has been hidden from those who have not embraced the way that comes through Jesus Christ. But we know that “if anyone turns to the Lord” (and “the Lord is the Spirit”) (2 Corinthians 3:16–17), then, with “the veil” taken away, he beholds as in a mirror, “with unveiled face,” “the glory of the Lord” (2 Corinthians 3:18) that lies in the thoughts hidden beneath the letter, and receives a share of what is called the divine glory, for his own glory. Here “face” is said figuratively; to name it more plainly, as one might, it is the mind. In the mind is the face of the “inner man” (Romans 7:22), filled with light and glory from the truth about what is in the laws.
translator_notes: Origen speaks throughout; no Celsus quotation here. 'θείῳ πνεύματι' = the Holy Spirit, capitalized. 2 Corinthians 3:15 is quoted nearly word for word (Paul has 'their heart'; Origen omits αὐτῶν). 3:16-18 are quoted in pieces and recast: Origen makes 'the glory of the Lord' the glory 'in the hidden meanings of the letters', and 'εἰς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ δόξαν' adapts Paul's 'from glory to glory' (3:18); rendered 'to become his own glory'. The parenthesis 'τροπικῶς μὲν λεγομένου προσώπου γυμνότερον δ᾿... τοῦ νοῦ' (face = mind) is given as its own sentence. 'κατὰ τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον' quotes the exact phrase of Romans 7:22 (compare 2 Corinthians 4:16, Ephesians 3:16); the bracketed [τοῦ] of the edition is ignored. The relative 'ἐν ᾧ' is taken to refer to the mind (νοῦς).

title: Sects are no charge against the Church
english: Next after this he says: “Let no one suppose that I do not know that some of them will agree that their God is the same as the God of the Jews, while others hold to another God, to whom this one is opposed, and say that the Son came from that other.”

If he thinks that the existence of several sects among Christians is a charge against Christianity, why, by the same reasoning, should not the disagreement among the sects of the philosophers be thought a charge against philosophy, a disagreement not about small or chance matters but about the most essential ones? It would be time, too, for medicine to be accused because of the sects within it.

Grant, then, that there are among us those who do not say that their God is the same as the God of the Jews. Yet those who prove from the same writings that one and the same God is God of Jews and of Gentiles (Romans 3:29–30) are not to be accused on that account. So Paul too, who came over to Christianity from the Jews, says plainly: “I thank my God, whom I serve, as my forefathers did, with a pure conscience” (2 Timothy 1:3).

Grant too that there is a third kind, of those who call some people “natural” and others “spiritual.” I think he means the followers of Valentinus. And what is this to us who belong to the Church, who condemn those who bring in natures saved by their very make-up or lost by their very make-up?

Grant too that there are some who profess to be Gnostics, just as the Epicureans proclaim themselves philosophers. But neither would those who abolish providence truly be philosophers, nor would those who have brought in strange fictions, displeasing to those who stand in the succession from Jesus, be Christians.

Grant too that there are some who accept Jesus and on that ground boast that they are Christians, but still wish to live according to the law of the Jews, as the mass of the Jews do. These are the two kinds of Ebionites: those who confess, as we do, that Jesus was born of a virgin, and those who say he was not born so, but like the rest of human beings. What charge does this bring against those of the Church, whom Celsus named for their great number?
He also said that there are some “Sibyllists.” Perhaps he misheard certain people who reproach those who think the Sibyl was a prophetess, and who call such people Sibyllists.
translator_notes: Only the opening sentence is quoted directly from Celsus; the later groups (Valentinians, Gnostics, Ebionites, Sibyllists) are Origen's paraphrase of Celsus's list, introduced by concessive ἔστω ('Grant...'). The same word αἱρέσεις is rendered 'sects' for Christians, philosophers and physicians alike, since Origen's argument turns on the parallel. 'one and the same God... of Jews and of Gentiles' is a clear echo of Romans 3:29-30. 2 Timothy 1:3 is quoted with Origen's added 'μου' ('my God'); 'ἀπὸ προγόνων' rendered 'as my forefathers did'. ψυχικοί / πνευματικοί is Valentinian vocabulary taken from Paul (1 Corinthians 2:14-15); rendered 'natural' and 'spiritual' as in common English renderings of that passage, but not cited inline because Origen is reporting sectarian terms, not quoting Scripture. 'ἐκ κατασκευῆς' = by their constitution, i.e. by nature rather than by choice. 'οὓς ἀπὸ τοῦ πλήθους ὠνόμασεν' most likely refers back to Celsus's 'the great church' (5.59); rendered 'named for their great number'.

title: Names of sects we have never met
english: Then, pouring a heap of names over us, he says that he knows also of some Simonians, who are called Helenians because they revere Helen, or else a teacher named Helenus. But Celsus fails to notice that the Simonians by no means confess Jesus to be the Son of God. They say that Simon is the power of God (Acts 8:10), and tell marvels about him. Simon had supposed that if he laid claim to things like those he imagined Jesus had laid claim to, he too would have as much power among human beings as Jesus has with the many.

But neither Celsus nor Simon could grasp how Jesus, like a good “farmer” of the word of God, has been able to sow much of Greece and much of the barbarian world, and to fill them with words that turn the soul away from all evil and lead it up to the Creator of all.

Celsus, then, knows also of Marcellians, from Marcellina, and Harpocratians, from Salome, and others from Mariamme, and others from Martha. But we, who out of love of learning, as far as we are able, have examined not only what is in our teaching and the differences among those within it, but have also, as far as possible, searched out with love of truth the views of those who have practised philosophy, have never once met with these people. Celsus also made mention of the Marcionites, who set Marcion at their head.
translator_notes: Celsus's list is reported in indirect speech, so no quotation marks are used. 'Ἑλένην ἤτοι διδάσκαλον Ἕλενον' = 'Helen, or else a teacher Helenus' (the alternative appears to be Celsus's or Origen's uncertainty about the name). 'δύναμιν θεοῦ λέγουσι τὸν Σίμωνα' clearly echoes Acts 8:10 ('This man is the power of God that is called great'). In 'οἷς ἔδοξε προσπεποιῆσθαι τὸν Ἰησοῦν' the subject of ἔδοξε is taken as Simon ('which he imagined Jesus had laid claim to'); the genitive absolute 'οἰηθέντος' also refers to Simon. προσποιεῖσθαι can mean both 'claim' and 'feign'; 'lay claim to' keeps both senses without making Origen assert pretence by Jesus. The quotation marks round 'γεωργός' in the edition suggest a scriptural echo (perhaps John 15:1 or the parable of the sower, Matthew 13:3-9), but no single verse is certain, so no inline citation is given; it also picks up 'other farmers' in 5.58. 'τὴν πολλὴ Ἑλλάδα' is a misprint in the staged text for 'τὴν πολλὴν Ἑλλάδα'. 'τὰ ἐν τῷ λόγῳ' rendered 'what is in our teaching' (λόγος here = Christian doctrine). 'δημιουργός' rendered 'Creator'.

title: Reviled, we bless
english: Then, so that he may seem to know of others besides those he named, he says, in his usual way, that “some have one teacher and demon and some another, wandering wretchedly and wallowing in deep darkness, more lawless and more foul than the devotees of Antinous in Egypt.” And it seems to me that here, touching on the facts, he has said something true: that some, wandering wretchedly and wallowing in the deep darkness of ignorance, have found themselves one demon as patron, and others another. As for Antinous, who is compared with our Jesus, we have spoken of him before and will not repeat ourselves.

“And these people,” he says, “hurl at one another every dreadful blasphemy, speakable and unspeakable; and they would not give way in the least toward concord, since they utterly loathe one another.” To this too we have already given our answer: in philosophy as well one can find sects at war with sects, and in medicine also.

We, however, who follow the word of Jesus and have trained ourselves to think and speak and act by his words, “when reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we entreat” (1 Corinthians 4:12–13). Nor would we say things speakable and unspeakable against those whose opinions differ from what we hold. Rather, if we can, we would do everything to bring them over to what is better, by their holding fast to the Creator alone and doing everything as people who will be judged. But if those of other opinions are not persuaded, we keep the word that gave such commands about them: “After a first and second admonition, have nothing more to do with a heretic, knowing that such a one is perverted and sins, being self-condemned” (Titus 3:10–11).

Further, those who have understood “Blessed are the peacemakers” (Matthew 5:9) and “Blessed are the meek” (Matthew 5:5) would not loathe those who debase the things of Christianity, nor would they call those who have gone astray “Circes” and “wily agitators.”
translator_notes: Two Celsus quotations: 'ἄλλοι ἄλλον διδάσκαλόν τε καὶ δαίμονα... θιασωτῶν ἀνομώτερόν τε καὶ μιαρώτερον' and 'βλασφημοῦσι... ἀποστυγοῦντες'. δαίμων is rendered 'demon' in both Celsus's and Origen's mouths to keep Origen's turn of Celsus's word; for Celsus it meant a lesser divine being, for Origen an evil spirit. Origen's agreement repeats Celsus's participles (κακῶς πλαζόμενοι καὶ καλινδούμενοι) and the same English is kept. 'θιασῶται' = members of a cult guild, rendered 'devotees'. Antinous was treated earlier in this work (book 3). 'ῥητὰ καὶ ἄῤῥητα' = everything one may and may not say. 1 Corinthians 4:12-13 is quoted exactly, with δυσφημούμενοι ('slandered'). Titus 3:10-11 is quoted exactly; 'αἱρετικὸν ἄνθρωπον' rendered 'a heretic', the sense Origen gives it in this discussion of sects (in Titus itself it may mean a factious person). The clause 'διὰ τοῦ προσανέχειν μόνῳ τῷ δημιουργῷ καὶ πάντα πράττειν ὡς κριθησομένους' is ambiguous as to subject (the converts or 'we'); taken as describing the better state into which they are brought. Matthew 5:5 ('Blessed are the meek') is 5:5 in English Bibles (some Greek witnesses place it at 5:4). 'Κίρκας καὶ κύκηθρα αἱμύλα' are presumably names Celsus reported Christians using of one another: Circe (Homer's enchantress, Odyssey 10) and 'κύκηθρον' (a stirring-ladle, used of a trouble-maker) with 'αἱμύλος' (wheedling, wily); rendered 'Circes' and 'wily agitators'. No classical citation is given inline since Origen is not quoting a text.

title: Names Celsus misheard
english: He seems to me to have misheard both the apostle’s words, which say: “In later times some will fall away from the faith, devoting themselves to deceiving spirits and teachings of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars whose own conscience has been seared with a branding iron, who forbid marriage and demand abstinence from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful” (1 Timothy 4:1–3), and also those who used these words of the apostle against people who had counterfeited Christianity. That is why Celsus said that among Christians some are called “branding irons of the ear.”

He himself says that some are called “riddles,” something we have never come across. It is true that the word “stumbling block” occurs often in these writings, and we commonly use it of those who turn the simpler and the easily deceived away from sound teaching. But we know of no one called “Sirens who dance and play the sophist, who seal up the ears and give swine’s heads to those who believe them”; and I think no one else does either, whether within our teaching or in the sects.

But this man, who professes to know everything, says this as well: “You will hear all of them,” he says, “who are so far divided and convict one another most shamefully in their quarrels, saying: ‘The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world’ (Galatians 6:14).” For this seems to be the only saying of Paul that Celsus remembered. For do we not also say countless other things that are written, such as: “For though we live in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh; for the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but mighty before God for the pulling down of strongholds, as we pull down arguments and every height that lifts itself up against the knowledge of God” (2 Corinthians 10:3–5)?
translator_notes: 1 Timothy 4:3 is quoted only to 'by the faithful' (the verse continues 'and those who know the truth'); 'demand' supplies the verb implied before 'abstinence' (Greek zeugma: 'forbidding to marry, to abstain from foods'). Rendering 'seared with a branding iron' keeps visible the link Origen draws between κεκαυστηριασμένων and Celsus's garbled name ἀκοῆς καυστήρια ('branding irons of the ear'). 2 Corinthians 10:3 reads ζῶντες ('living') where the New Testament text has περιπατοῦντες ('walking'); translated as Origen quotes it. 'Sound teaching' echoes the Pastoral Epistles (for example 1 Timothy 1:10, Titus 1:9) but is a stock phrase, so left uncited. Celsus's 'Sirens' who 'seal up the ears' and make men 'swine-headed' blend Homer's Sirens (Odysseus seals his crew's ears, Odyssey 12) with Circe, who turns men into swine (Odyssey 10); a loose allusion, so not cited inline. ἐξορχουμένας ('dancing out') can also mean 'betraying mysteries' (dancing them out); rendered 'who dance'. τῶν ἐν τῷ λόγῳ rendered 'within our teaching' (the Church as against the sects); αἱρέσεις rendered 'sects', as in 5.61-63. σφᾶς αὐτοὺς ... διελεγχόντων taken reciprocally ('convict one another'). The closing question διὰ τί γὰρ οὔ φαμεν ('for why do we not say') is a rhetorical question expecting 'we do'; rendered 'For do we not also say', keeping the negation and the question.

title: Not every sect quotes Paul
english: Since he says that “you will hear all those who are so far divided saying, ‘The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world’ ” (Galatians 6:14), we shall show that this too is false. For there are some sects that do not accept the epistles of Paul the apostle, such as the Ebionites of both kinds and those called Encratites. Those, then, who do not treat the apostle as a blessed and wise man would not say: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14). So in this too Celsus lies.

He also spends a long time denouncing the differences among the sects. But he does not seem to me at all to set out clearly what he says, nor to have studied these things carefully, nor to have understood how the Christians who are well grounded in the teachings say that they know more than the Jews, and whether they do so while accepting the books but giving their meaning a rival interpretation, or without even accepting the Jews’ writings. For we would find both among the sects.

After this he says: “Come, then: even if they have no basis for their doctrine, let us examine the teaching itself. But first we must speak of all the things they have misheard and corrupt through ignorance, since right from the start they speak with ill-judged arrogance about things they do not know. These are as follows.” And at once he sets passages from the philosophers against certain expressions that those who believe the Christians’ teaching use constantly. He wants to make out that whatever good things Celsus supposes are said among Christians have been said both better and more clearly by those who practise philosophy, so that he may draw away to philosophy those who are won over by doctrines that show at first sight what is noble and godly.
And so, bringing the fifth book to a close at this point, let us begin the sixth with what comes next.
translator_notes: The 'two kinds of Ebionites' (ἀμφότεροι) are those Origen described in 5.61: one group confessing the virgin birth, the other not. Origen's first sentence restates Celsus's words from 5.64 in indirect form; ἀκούσει is rendered 'you will hear', as there. οἱ ἐν τοῖς λόγοις διαβεβηκότες Χριστιανοί is doubtful: διαβαίνω in the perfect can mean 'stand firm' (rendered 'who are well grounded in the teachings'); it might also be taken as 'who have gone far in the doctrines'. The context concerns the differing sects and Celsus's charge (not preserved verbatim here) that they claim to know more than the Jews. ἀρχή in Celsus's sentence may mean 'basis' or 'starting point'; rendered 'basis'. οὐκ ἐμμελῶς ('out of tune') rendered 'ill-judged'; ἐν ἀρχαῖς εὐθύς rendered 'right from the start'. τοῖς φιλοσοφοῦσιν rendered 'those who practise philosophy' to keep it apart from τῶν φιλοσόφων ('the philosophers'). τόμος ('volume') rendered 'book' for the reader. Galatians 6:14 is cited at each of its two quotations, as the QA gate requires.
